title: Mixing coloured light: why a red torch and a green torch make a yellow wall

summary.text: Shine a red torch and a green torch on one white wall, and the wall looks yellow, though no yellow light is anywhere in the room. Hold a pencil in front, and its two shadows are not grey. One is red and one is green. Your child tests how coloured lights add up, how filters and inks take colours away, and why three kinds of colour cells in the eye are enough to build every colour on a phone screen. Nobody yet knows how three signals in the brain become the feeling of yellow.
summary.art: A dim room with a red torch and a green torch shining on a white wall, a glowing yellow patch in the middle where the beams overlap, and a pencil in front of the wall with one red shadow and one green shadow.

intro.hook: Switch off the room light. Shine a red torch on a white wall. Now add a green torch on the same spot. What colour is the spot now? Most people are sure they know. Most people are wrong.
intro.text: Red light plus green light makes yellow. But red paint plus green paint makes a muddy brown. Lights and paints seem to follow opposite rules. In this unit you find out why. You make coloured shadows, stack coloured inks, and light up objects with coloured torches. You will see a coloured thing turn almost black, and a white wall turn yellow with no yellow light anywhere. Then you meet the real puzzle. The yellow is not in the room. So where is it?
intro.art: A child in a dark room holding two torches, one with red cellophane and one with green, both pointing at a white wall that glows yellow where the beams meet.

outcomes: I can predict the colour made when two or three coloured lights shine on one white spot: red and green make yellow, red and blue make magenta, green and blue make cyan, and all three make white.
I can explain why a pencil's shadow turns red or green when two coloured lights shine on it.
I can explain that a filter, an ink or a paint takes colours away from white light, so mixing them makes the colour darker.
I can say why a coloured thing can look bright in one coloured light and almost black in another.
I can explain that most eyes have three kinds of colour-sensing cells, and that this is why three lights can make every colour on a screen.
I can explain why tiny dots of two colours blend into a third colour when I stand far enough away.
I can fill in a results table, compare it with my guess, and finish with claim, evidence and reasoning.
I can say what scientists agree about mixing colours, and what nobody knows yet.

terms.meaning: Mixing coloured lights by shining them on the same spot. Each light adds more light, so the mix is brighter than each one alone.
terms.example: A red torch and a green torch on one white wall make a yellow patch that is brighter than either torch alone.
terms.art: Two circles of coloured light overlapping on a white wall, red and green, with a bright yellow patch where they meet.

terms.meaning: Red, green and blue. They are the three lights that can be mixed to make nearly every other colour we see.
terms.example: A phone screen makes all its colours from tiny red, green and blue dots.
terms.art: Three overlapping circles of light, red, green and blue, with white in the middle.

terms.meaning: The colours made by mixing two primary lights. Red and green make yellow. Green and blue make cyan. Red and blue make magenta.
terms.example: A stage lit by a green lamp and a blue lamp together glows a bright blue-green.
terms.art: Three overlapping light circles with yellow, cyan and magenta labelled in the overlaps.

terms.meaning: A bright blue-green, like the colour of a clear tropical sea. It is the colour you get from green light plus blue light.
terms.example: The blue-green ink in a colour printer is cyan.
terms.art: A swatch of bright blue-green next to a glass of clear sea water.

terms.meaning: A bright pink-purple. It is made by red light plus blue light, with no green. It is not in the rainbow.
terms.example: The flowers of a bougainvillea plant are often magenta.
terms.art: A bougainvillea branch with bright pink-purple flowers on a white wall.

terms.meaning: Mixing filters, inks or paints. Each one takes some colours away from white light, so the mix is darker than each one alone.
terms.example: Yellow highlighter over blue highlighter makes green that is darker than either.
terms.art: A white page with a yellow stripe and a blue stripe crossing, the crossing square dark green.

terms.meaning: A see-through sheet that lets some colours of light through and takes the rest away.
terms.example: Red cellophane lets red light through and takes most other colours away.
terms.art: A torch beam passing through a sheet of red cellophane and coming out red.

terms.meaning: A coloured substance that soaks into cloth, paper or hair. It takes some colours out of the light that falls on it and sends the rest back to your eyes.
terms.example: Indigo dye makes cloth look blue because it takes away most red and yellow light.
terms.art: A hand lifting a blue cloth out of a clay pot of dye.

terms.meaning: One of the colour-sensing cells in the retina. Most people have three kinds, and each kind responds best to a different part of the rainbow.
terms.example: Your cone cells are working right now as you read this page in daylight.
terms.art: A drawing of a retina with cone cells in three shades: one reddish, one greenish and one bluish.

terms.meaning: One tiny spot of a screen picture. On most screens each pixel is a small group of one red, one green and one blue dot.
terms.example: If you look at a phone screen through a strong magnifier, you can see the tiny coloured dots of each pixel.
terms.art: A magnified patch of a phone screen showing tiny red, green and blue dots in a repeating pattern.

terms.meaning: A shadow that is not grey. It happens when two lights of different colours shine on a thing from different sides.
terms.example: Under a red lamp and a green lamp, a pencil makes one red shadow and one green shadow.
terms.art: A pencil in front of a white wall with a red shadow on the left and a green shadow on the right.

terms.meaning: Two colours of light that make white when added together, such as red and cyan. In paint they are pairs that make a dull grey-brown.
terms.example: On the colour circle, yellow sits opposite blue.
terms.art: A circle divided into six coloured slices with arrows joining opposite slices.

terms.meaning: A ghost of a colour that you still see for a few seconds after you stop looking at something bright or strongly coloured.
terms.example: After staring at a bright green leaf, you may see a pink leaf shape on a white wall.
terms.art: A child looking at a white wall where a faint pink leaf shape floats.

terms.meaning: Colours blending in your eye because tiny dots of different colours are too small to tell apart.
terms.example: From across a room, close red and green dots look yellow-brown.
terms.art: A grid of red and green dots, close up, and the same grid as one smooth patch from far away.

terms.meaning: A way of printing a picture with tiny dots of a few inks. From far away, the dots blend into a picture with many colours.
terms.example: A colour newspaper photo is made of tiny dots when you look at it with a magnifying glass.
terms.art: A newspaper photo with a circle magnified to show cyan, magenta, yellow and black dots.

terms.meaning: A way of seeing colour that is different from most people's, often because one kind of cone cell works differently. It is also called colour blindness.
terms.example: Some people find it hard to tell a red tomato from a green one on a plate.
terms.art: Two plates of fruit, one as most people see it and one with red and green looking alike.

terms.meaning: What we see when almost no light comes to the eye from a place. A black object takes in nearly all the light that falls on it.
terms.example: A black dosa tawa takes in nearly all the light that falls on it.
terms.art: A black tawa on a stove next to a white plate in the same light.

explanations.definition: When coloured lights shine on the same spot, their light adds up. Red plus green makes yellow, green plus blue makes cyan, red plus blue makes magenta, and all three together make white.
explanations.description: Take a white wall in a dim room. Shine a red torch on it, and the wall looks red. Add a green torch on the same spot, and the spot turns yellow. Add a blue torch too, and it turns white. Each torch adds more light, so the spot gets brighter each time. This is called additive mixing. The wall does not change. The light that reaches your eye changes. Stage lamps, phone screens and LED strip lights all use it. They need only red, green and blue lamps to make almost every colour.
examples: Red and green stage lamps lighting the same curtain make it look yellow.
A strip of coloured LED lights in a shop window changes colour by changing how bright its red, green and blue lamps are.
A phone screen shows white when its red, green and blue dots all shine together.
explanations.art: A white wall with three circles of light, red, green and blue, overlapping, with labels for yellow, cyan, magenta and white.
explanations.context: You may think mixing means getting muddy. This card shows the other kind of mixing, where colours get brighter.

explanations.concept: Why red and green lights look yellow
explanations.definition: The eye has three kinds of colour cells. Red light plus green light excites them in nearly the same way as real yellow light does, so we see yellow.
explanations.description: Real yellow light has its own wavelength, between green and orange in the rainbow. A lemon lit by sunshine sends some of this light to your eyes. But the eye does not measure wavelengths. It has three kinds of cone cells, and each kind reports how much light it caught. Real yellow light makes the red-sensing and green-sensing cones respond a lot. A red torch and a green torch together make those same two kinds respond a lot too. The brain gets the same signals, so you see the same yellow. A machine that measures wavelengths could tell the two apart at once. Your eyes cannot.
examples: A phone screen shows yellow using only its red and green dots. Its yellow looks the same as a banana's yellow.
A lemon lit by sunshine and a screen showing yellow look alike, though the light from each is very different.
A device called a spectrometer splits light by wavelength, and it shows that the screen's yellow and the lemon's yellow are not the same.
explanations.art: Two eyes viewing a lemon and a phone screen showing yellow, with arrows to the same three cone signals and a speech bubble saying yellow.
explanations.context: The red and green torches made a yellow wall. This card explains where the yellow came from, if it is not in the torches.

explanations.definition: When two lights of different colours shine on a thing from different sides, each shadow is lit by the other light, so each shadow has the colour of the other light.
explanations.description: A shadow is a place where a light is blocked. With one white torch, the shadow is dark, because no light reaches it. With a red torch and a green torch, the pencil blocks the red light on one side. Only green light reaches that patch, so the shadow looks green. On the other side the pencil blocks the green light. Only red reaches that patch, so the shadow looks red. Where both lights reach, the wall looks yellow. If you add a blue torch as well, the shadows turn cyan, magenta and yellow, and the lit wall looks white.
examples: On a stage lit from both sides by a red lamp and a blue lamp, a dancer's two shadows look blue and red.
In a room lit by a tubelight and a warm yellowish lamp, shadows have a faint bluish or yellowish edge.
Theatre lighting designers put coloured lamps on both sides of the stage on purpose, so that actors have coloured shadows.
explanations.art: A pencil in front of a white wall lit from the left by a red torch and from the right by a green torch, with the green shadow and red shadow labelled.
explanations.context: The two torch test showed coloured shadows. This card says why each shadow has the colour it has.

explanations.definition: A colour filter lets some colours of light through and takes the others away. Two filters together take away even more.
explanations.description: White light holds every colour. A red filter lets red light through and takes most of the other colours away. The filter does not make red light. It only decides what to let through. A green filter lets green through. Put a red filter and a green filter together, and almost no light gets past both. The light is mostly dark. A cyan filter lets green and blue through. A yellow filter lets red and green through. Put those two together, and only green gets through both. This is called subtractive mixing, because each layer subtracts, or takes away, some light.
examples: A yellow sheet over a cyan sheet in front of a torch gives a green patch.
Red cellophane plus green cellophane in front of a torch gives a patch that is almost dark.
Sunglasses with coloured lenses make everything look tinted, because they take some colours away.
explanations.art: A torch beam passing through one yellow and one cyan filter, with arrows showing red, green and blue light entering and only green coming out.
explanations.context: Lights add colours together. This card is about the opposite thing: sheets that take colours away.

explanations.definition: Inks, dyes and paints are made of tiny coloured grains or molecules. Each kind takes some colours out of the light and sends the rest back. Mixing them takes away more colours, so the mix is darker.
explanations.description: A yellow paint sends back red and green and takes away blue. A cyan paint sends back green and blue and takes away red. Mix them and only green is sent back by both, so you get green. But it is a darker green than either paint, because each paint took away some light. Cyan, magenta and yellow are the three colours that mix best for paint and ink. A colour printer uses these three inks and adds black ink. Mixing all three gives a dark muddy colour, not a true black, so black ink is added. Red, yellow and blue paints, as many children learn, also work but make a smaller range of colours.
examples: A colour printer makes all its pictures from cyan, magenta, yellow and black ink.
Mixing many paints from a school box makes a dark brown.
A pink highlighter over a yellow highlighter makes an orange-red.
explanations.art: A colour printer cartridge with four small tanks of cyan, magenta, yellow and black ink, and a page with overlapping squares of the three colours.
explanations.context: Paints seem to behave oppositely from lights. This card explains why.

explanations.concept: Why a thing can look bright in one light and dark in another
explanations.definition: A coloured thing sends back only the colours it does not take away. If those colours are missing from the light that falls on it, the thing looks dark.
explanations.description: A green leaf takes away most red and blue and sends back green. In sunlight, which holds every colour, it looks green. In a pure red light there is almost no green for the leaf to send back, so the leaf looks nearly black. A yellow cloth sends back red and green but takes away blue. In red light it looks bright red. In green light it looks bright green. In blue light it looks dark. A white thing sends back every colour, so it takes on whatever colour the light has. A black thing takes away nearly all of every colour, so it looks black in every light.
examples: A green leaf looks nearly black under a red bulb.
A white sheet under a blue bulb looks blue.
Under the orange street lights some cities use, a red car and a blue car can look much alike.
explanations.art: A grid of five coloured papers under red, green and blue light, with the bright ones glowing and the dark ones nearly black.
explanations.context: In an earlier unit, a leaf turned dark under red light. This card turns that single surprise into a rule that you can use for any colour.

explanations.definition: Two colours of light that make white together are complementary, such as red and cyan. After staring at one colour, you may see its complement for a few seconds.
explanations.description: Stare at a bright green shape for half a minute, then look at a white wall. You may see a pink shape. The cone cells that sense green have been working hard, and they tire. When you look at white, those cells answer a little less than usual, while the other kinds answer as usual. So the white looks a little pinker for a moment. Stare at a cyan stripe and you see a faint red one. This is an afterimage. It is made in the eye, not on the wall. It fades in a few seconds as the tired cells rest.
examples: After a bright camera flash, you may see a dark spot, then a coloured spot, for a few seconds.
After staring at a blue-green stripe, you see a faint red-orange stripe on a white wall.
Surgical gowns are often green or blue, which is said to rest eyes that have stared at red for a long time.
explanations.art: A cyan stripe flag and the faint orange-white-green flag appearing on a white wall, with arrows showing tired cells in the retina.
explanations.context: You will test this on a flag. This card says why the colours flip.

explanations.definition: When coloured dots are too small and too close to see separately, their light blends in your eye into one colour.
explanations.description: Your eye can only tell two dots apart if they are far enough apart. Closer than that, their light lands on the same cells and mixes. A colour newspaper photo has tiny dots of cyan, magenta, yellow and black ink. From a normal distance the dots blend, and you see a picture with every colour. A screen is the same. It has tiny red, green and blue dots. Painters have used this too. Georges Seurat, a French painter, built whole paintings from small dots of paint in the 1880s. Step back from a dot painting and the colours blend. Step close and they fall apart again.
examples: A colour newspaper picture is a pattern of tiny dots when you look at it with a magnifier.
A kolam made with dots of two colours of rangoli powder looks like a third colour from a few steps away.
A TV looks like a smooth picture from the sofa and like coloured dots from one centimetre away.
explanations.art: A dot painting seen close up as separate coloured dots, and from far away as a smooth picture of a garden.
explanations.context: Dots on paper and dots on a screen both make colours in your eye. This card explains how.

explanations.concept: The brain adjusts for the colour of light
explanations.definition: Your brain tries to guess the true colour of a thing, even when the light changes. Scientists call this colour constancy, and they are still working out exactly how it is done.
explanations.description: A white sheet looks white in sunlight. It also looks white under a yellowish bulb, though the light reaching your eye is much yellower. Your brain notices the colour of the light and takes it into account. It looks at the whole scene, not at one patch. This is why a sari in a shop may look one colour under the shop lights and a slightly different one when you carry it to the door. Cameras do a similar job with a setting called white balance. Nobody yet knows exactly how the brain does it. In 2015, a photo of a dress went around the world, and people argued about whether it was blue and black or white and gold. Their brains had guessed different lights.
examples: A white wall looks white in the morning and still looks white in the evening, though the light is yellower.
A phone camera sometimes makes photos look too yellow indoors until its white balance catches up.
A shopkeeper takes a sari to the door to show its colour in daylight.
explanations.art: A white sheet lit by a yellow lamp and the same sheet in daylight, both drawn white, with an eye and a brain between them.
explanations.context: A white thing is not always the same colour of light to your eye, yet you see it as white. This card says what your brain does.

explanations.definition: People and animals have different numbers of cone cell types, so they see colour differently. Most people have three. Dogs have two. Many birds have four.
explanations.description: A dog has two kinds of cone cells, so a dog tells yellow and blue well, but mixes up red and green. Many birds have four kinds, and one of them senses ultraviolet. In many countries, about 1 boy or man in 12 and about 1 girl or woman in 200 has a colour vision difference. In most cases one of the three kinds of cone works differently, so some reds and greens look alike. It is not an illness. It is a different way of seeing. Even among people with three kinds of cone, the exact response of each kind varies a little, so no two people see colour in exactly the same way. A test with dotted number pictures, designed by Shinobu Ishihara in Japan more than 100 years ago, is still used to find out.
examples: A dog does not see a red ball on green grass as clearly as a human does.
A person with red-green colour blindness may sort a red crayon with the brown ones.
A peacock's feathers reflect some ultraviolet light, which peafowl can probably see and we cannot.
explanations.art: A dog, a person and a bird each looking at a flower, with three different pictures of the flower in thought bubbles.
explanations.context: Not everyone sees colour the same way. This card says how eyes differ.

explanations.concept: Is yellow in the light or in us?
explanations.description: A red torch and a green torch together look yellow, and a real yellow lamp looks yellow too. So is yellow a property of the light, or of the eye, or of the brain? People who study this give different answers. Everyone agrees on the measurements. The disagreement is about what we mean when we say a colour is there.
examples: A banana looks yellow in daylight and nearly black in blue light.
A screen shows a yellow sunflower using only red and green dots.
Two people may call the same wall yellow and still see it slightly differently.

perspectives.explanation: Colour is a name for a mix of wavelengths. Yellow light has its own wavelength. Red plus green is a different mix that happens to fool our eyes.
Colour is what the eye and brain make from the light. The same signals make the same yellow, whatever the light was. So yellow is a result in us, caused by light.
Even if we know every wavelength and every signal, we may not know what yellow feels like. Nobody can check whether yours feels the same as mine.

explanations.art: A yellow wall with three people looking at it, each with a different thought bubble: wavelengths, cone signals and a feeling.
explanations.context: The unit ends with a puzzle: the yellow was not in the room. This card gives the main answers people have.

agreed.text: Red, green and blue lights mixed together can make almost every colour, including white.
agreed.evidence: Stage lamps, LED strips and screens do it every day, and people matching colours with three lights get very close.

agreed.text: Most people have three kinds of cone cell, and a colour is built from comparing their three signals.
agreed.evidence: Thomas Young guessed it in 1802. By 1980 scientists had measured the light that each kind of cone catches in human retinas.

agreed.text: Filters, inks and paints take colours away, so mixing them makes things darker.
agreed.evidence: Stacked cellophane sheets and layered highlighters get darker with each layer, and a lightmeter shows less light getting through.

agreed.text: Different mixes of light can look the same to us.
agreed.evidence: A spectrometer shows that a yellow lamp and a red-plus-green screen have different wavelengths, yet people cannot tell them apart.

agreed.text: Colour vision differs between people and between animals.
agreed.evidence: Colour tests find people who confuse red and green. Behaviour tests and measurements of retinas show that dogs have two kinds of cone and many birds have four.

agreed.text: Coloured shadows happen whenever lights of different colours shine on a thing from different sides.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can repeat the two torch test, and theatre lighting designers use coloured shadows on purpose.

challenging.claim: Red, yellow and blue are the three basic colours that mix to make all the others.
challenging.who: Many art teachers and school books for hundreds of years.
challenging.for: Painters can make many colours from red, yellow and blue paints, and the idea is easy to teach.
challenging.against: Cyan, magenta and yellow make a much wider range of colours when mixed as paint or ink, and printers use them. For light, red, green and blue work best. There is no single set of basic colours for everything.

challenging.claim: Mixing colours always makes a darker colour.
challenging.who: Many people who only ever mix paints.
challenging.for: Every time you mix more paints, the colour does get darker.
challenging.against: When you mix coloured lights, each light adds more light, so the mix gets brighter. Red and green light together are brighter than either.

challenging.claim: A screen with red, green and blue can show every colour the eye can see.
challenging.who: Many people, including many who sell screens.
challenging.for: Screens show a huge range of colours, and nearly all the colours of everyday life.
challenging.against: A pure green or blue-green from a laser or a rainbow is more intense than any screen can make. Screens can show most colours, but not all.

challenging.claim: Brown is a colour of its own, like red or blue.
challenging.for: Brown looks as different from orange as green looks from blue, and we have a separate word for it.
challenging.against: Vision scientists find that brown is dim orange or yellow seen next to brighter things. A patch of orange light on a dark wall looks orange, and the same colour in a bright room looks brown.

challenging.claim: Black and white are not colours.
challenging.for: Black means no light and white means all colours together, so they seem to lack colour.
challenging.against: People use both as colours in everyday life, and vision scientists treat the brightness of a colour as part of the colour. Whether to call them colours is partly a choice of words.

challenging.claim: Everyone sees colours exactly the same way.
challenging.who: Many people who have never compared notes.
challenging.for: Most people agree on the names of colours, and most people have three kinds of cone cell.
challenging.against: About 1 boy or man in 12 sees some reds and greens differently. Even people with three kinds of cone have slightly different cones. Nobody can compare the feeling of colour from the inside.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, painters taught that red, yellow and blue are the three basic colours, and that every other colour is a mix of them. In 1802, Thomas Young in England suggested something different for light. He guessed that the eye has only three kinds of detector, so three lights might be enough to make any colour. In the 1850s, James Clerk Maxwell, a Scottish scientist, tested the idea. He built a box of coloured lights and asked people to match colours by changing just three of them. Three were enough. In 1861, he showed a picture of a tartan ribbon. It was made from three black and white photographs, taken through red, green and blue filters, and then shone back through the same filters on one screen. The ribbon appeared in colour. For paints, the old rule is a useful guide. For light, the three that work best are red, green and blue.
how_we_found_out.who: Thomas Young and James Clerk Maxwell
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Red, yellow and blue are the only three basic colours for everything. Maxwell's tartan ribbon, made from three filtered pictures, showed that red, green and blue light can make the full range of colour.

big_questions.q: A red torch and a green torch make a yellow wall, but there is no yellow light anywhere. Is the wall really yellow?
big_questions.hint: Think about what reached your eye, and what your eye does with it.

big_questions.q: Mixing lights makes things brighter, and mixing paints makes things darker. Why would mixing do opposite things?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each torch adds, and what each paint takes away.

big_questions.q: A dog has two kinds of cone cell and you have three. Does a dog see fewer colours, or different colours?
big_questions.hint: A dog is good at some things we are bad at. Think about why that might matter to a dog.

big_questions.q: Every colour on a phone screen is made from only three. Does that mean every colour in the world is made from three?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the screen is copying, and what it is making from scratch.

big_questions.q: A sari looks one colour in the shop and another at the door. Which one is its true colour?
big_questions.hint: Think about who decides what the true colour is, and what the light does.

big_questions.q: Hot stars look blue and cooler stars look red, but we call red a warm colour. Why does it feel backwards?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the words warm and cool come from, and what your eye reports.

big_questions.q: If a picture is made of three kinds of dots, where is the picture: in the dots or in your head?
big_questions.hint: Walk away from the picture until the dots vanish. What changed?

big_questions.q: Can you imagine a colour you have never seen? What does your answer say about where colours live?
big_questions.hint: Try it, and notice what you picture.

big_questions.q: Who decides which three colours are the primary colours: nature, our eyes, or us?
big_questions.hint: Think about why the answer is different for lights and for paints.

big_questions.q: A friend with red-green colour blindness sees a map differently from you. Who sees the map correctly?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the map is for, and who made it.

story.title: The Sunrise With No Yellow Bulb
story.note: A made-up story. The science in it is real. Red and green light shining on the same white surface look yellow. A green cloth lit only by red light looks almost black. Stage lamps in red, green and blue are used in many theatres. The school, the play, Ilakkiya, her aunt and everyone else in the story are made up.
text: Ilakkiya was ten, and on the afternoon before Pongal she was the only person in the school hall who was not shouting.

The school was a small one, near Thanjavur, with paddy fields on three sides. Tomorrow it would put on a play called The Sun Comes to the Paddy. Twelve children were dressed as paddy plants, in green skirts and green scarves. One small boy was the Sun, in a bright yellow shawl. At the end of the play, the Sun was meant to rise slowly over the field, and the whole stage was meant to glow gold.

Ilakkiya's aunt ran a shop called Selvi Light and Sound Service. She hired out speakers and lamps for weddings and festivals. That week she had brought a big box of stage lamps to the school. There was a red lamp, a green lamp, a blue lamp and one fat yellow lamp for the Sun. Ilakkiya's job was to hold the ladder.
Then the yellow lamp went pop.

A thin line of smoke curled up from it, and the whole hall went quiet. Aunt Selvi flicked the switch twice. Nothing. "The spare is in my shop," she said slowly. "The shop is twelve kilometres away, and the last bus has gone."

The school electrician, Murugesan Anna, scratched his head. "No yellow lamp, no golden Sun," he said. "We must change the ending. The Sun will rise in plain white light, and that is that." The headmistress looked sad. The twelve paddy plants looked sadder. They had practised for a month.
"We do not need a yellow lamp," said Ilakkiya.
Murugesan Anna laughed, but kindly. "Child, the Sun is yellow."

Ilakkiya did not argue. She just remembered a kitchen wall. The week before, she had wrapped a red sweet wrapper over one torch and a green one over another, only to see what would happen. When she pointed both at the wall, the wall had turned a warm yellow. She had stared at it for a long time.
"Please switch on the red lamp and the green lamp," she said. "Only those two. Point both at the white curtain at the back."

Murugesan Anna did it, mostly to make her happy. The red lamp lit one round patch of the curtain red. The green lamp lit another patch green. And where the two patches overlapped, the curtain glowed a warm, golden yellow.
Murugesan Anna looked at the curtain. Then he looked at the lamps. Then he looked at the curtain again. "There is no yellow in those lamps," he said.
"Don't look at the lamps, Anna," said Ilakkiya. "Look at the curtain."
Aunt Selvi began to laugh so loudly that the paddy plants turned round. "I have sold lamps for twenty years," she said, "and I never once tried it!"

But a second trouble came at once. When Ilakkiya tested the red lamp alone, to see what dawn would look like, a girl in a green skirt shrieked. "Our skirts have gone black!" And it was true. In pure red light, the green cloth looked nearly black.

Ilakkiya thought hard. Green cloth could only send back the green light that fell on it. A red lamp had no green in it. So the skirts had nothing to send back. Then she smiled. "The play begins before sunrise," she said. "It should be dark. Let the field be dark at first!"

She wrote the plan on the back of her hand. First, only the red lamp. The field would be dark, and the Sun, in his yellow shawl, would look like a small red ball at the edge. Next, the green lamp. The curtain would turn yellow, the paddy would turn green again, and the Sun's shawl would shine gold. Last, the blue lamp, and the whole stage would blaze white, like noon.
On Pongal evening the hall was full. The lights dimmed. Only the red lamp glowed, and twelve dark shapes stood very still in a red field, with a small red Sun at the edge. Nobody breathed.

Then Murugesan Anna, who had been told to wait for Ilakkiya's nod, switched on the green lamp. A golden light spread across the stage. The paddy turned green, one skirt after another, as if the whole field were waking up. The Sun's shawl blazed gold. A moment later the blue lamp came on, and the whole stage shone as bright as noon. The audience clapped before the song had even started.
Afterwards, Murugesan Anna came to find her. "One question," he said. "There is no yellow in the lamps. There is no yellow in the curtain. It is only white cloth. So where did the yellow come from?"

Ilakkiya thought about it for a long time. "The red and the green both landed in the same place," she said slowly. "My eyes answered the way they would answer to yellow. I think the yellow was made inside us." She grinned. "But I don't know how. Ask me when I am eleven."
story.epiphany: For the parent: red light and green light landing on the same white curtain look yellow, because the eye has three kinds of colour cells, and red plus green excites them in nearly the same way as real yellow light does. So the stage did not need a yellow lamp. A green cloth lit by pure red light looks almost black, because the cloth has no green light to send back.
ask: A red lamp and a green lamp together lit a white curtain yellow. Where was the yellow made?
A green cloth looks nearly black under a red lamp. What does that tell you about where a thing's colour comes from?
If you had only a red, a green and a blue lamp, how would you light a pink sky at sunset?
A white curtain can look red, yellow, green or white. What does the curtain itself do, and what does the light do?

games.title: Add or Take Away? Guess the colour
games.context: This is a guessing game about colours. Each card describes lights or inks being mixed. You decide if the colours add or are taken away, and guess the colour that results.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards in a shuffled pile with their fronts showing, and eight tokens in two kinds laid out in front of the players.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud while the other players each put a token face down in front of them.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Everyone else picks a token.

setup.art: All the tokens turned over together and the reader turning the card to read the answer on the back.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over together. Then read the back.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: a mix of lights, filters or inks on the front, and the answer on the back

items.f: A red torch and a green torch shine on the same spot of a white wall.
items.b: Lights add. The spot looks yellow, and it is brighter than either torch alone.

items.f: A green torch and a blue torch shine on one spot of a white wall.
items.b: Lights add. The spot looks cyan, a bright blue-green.

items.f: A red torch and a blue torch shine on one spot of a white wall.
items.b: Lights add. The spot looks magenta, a bright pink-purple.

items.f: Red, green and blue torches all shine on one spot of a white wall.
items.b: Lights add. The spot looks white, or nearly white.

items.f: A phone screen shows white.
items.b: Lights add. Tiny red, green and blue dots shine together, and your eye sees white.

items.f: A phone screen shows bright yellow.
items.b: Lights add. Only the red and green dots are lit. Your eye cannot tell this from real yellow light.

items.f: A stage curtain is lit by a red lamp and a blue lamp at the same time.
items.b: Lights add. The curtain looks magenta.

items.f: Two red torches shine on the same spot of a white wall.
items.b: Lights add. The spot is still red, but brighter than with one torch.

items.f: A paper disc with red and green slices spins very fast.
items.b: Lights add in your eye. The colours blend into a dull yellowish colour.

items.f: Tiny yellow and blue dots sit side by side and are seen from far away.
items.b: Lights add in your eye. The dots blend into a pale, greyish colour, not into green.

items.f: A red lamp and a cyan lamp light the same white wall.
items.b: Lights add. Cyan is green plus blue, so the wall gets all three colours and looks white.

items.f: First a red lamp, then a green lamp is also switched on, lighting the same curtain.
items.b: Lights add. The curtain looks red at first, then yellow.

items.f: A yellow highlighter is coloured over a blue highlighter on white paper.
items.b: Taken away. Each ink takes colours away from the light. The mix looks green, and darker than either.

items.f: Red cellophane is held in front of a white torch.
items.b: Taken away. The cellophane takes most colours away, so the light is red.

items.f: Red cellophane and green cellophane are held together in front of a white torch.
items.b: Taken away. Very little light gets past both sheets, so the patch looks nearly dark.

items.f: Yellow paint and blue paint are stirred together.
items.b: Taken away. Each paint takes colours away. The mix looks green, and darker than either paint.

items.f: Every colour from a school paint box is stirred into one pot.
items.b: Taken away. Each paint takes away some of the light, so almost none comes back. The mix looks dark brown.

items.f: A cyan sheet and a yellow sheet are held together in front of a white torch.
items.b: Taken away. Cyan lets green and blue through and yellow lets red and green through. Only green gets past both.

items.f: A magenta sheet and a yellow sheet are held together in front of a white torch.
items.b: Taken away. Magenta lets red and blue through and yellow lets red and green through. Only red gets past both.

items.f: A green leaf is lit by a red torch only.
items.b: Taken away. The leaf takes the red light away and has no green to send back. It looks nearly black.

items.f: A colour printer prints cyan, magenta and yellow ink on the same spot of a page.
items.b: Taken away. Each ink takes colours away, so the spot looks dark and muddy. That is why printers add black ink.

items.f: Two sheets of the same yellow cellophane are held in front of a white torch.
items.b: Taken away. The second sheet takes away more light, so the patch is a deeper yellow and dimmer.

items.f: A white shirt is dipped in a pot of blue dye.
items.b: Taken away. The dye takes away red and yellow light. The shirt sends back mostly blue.

items.f: Sunlight shines through a green glass bottle onto a table.
items.b: Taken away. The glass lets only the green through and takes most of the other colours away. A green patch lands on the table.

printables.title: 8 tokens: four that say LIGHTS ADD and four that say COLOURS TAKEN AWAY

rules: Cut out the 24 cards and the 8 tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile with the fronts showing. Each player takes one LIGHTS ADD token and one COLOURS TAKEN AWAY token.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud, but keeps the back hidden.
Every other player chooses a token and puts it face down. Each also decides on the colour they think will result.
When everyone is ready, turn the tokens over together. Each player says their colour aloud. Then the reader reads the back.
A player who chose the right token scores 1 point. A player who also named the right colour, or said it would be dark, scores 1 more point.
The next player to the left becomes the reader, and the game goes on. In a game for two players, you take turns to be the reader.
When the pile runs out, count the points. The player with the most points wins. If two players have the same, they share the win.
If nobody was right on a card, the reader reads the back again, and the group talks about why before the next card.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile with the fronts showing. Give each player one token of each kind. No printer? Copy each card on a paper slip, with the front on one side and the answer on the other. Use two kinds of bottle caps or coins as the tokens.
flow.say: These cards describe lights, filters or paints being mixed. Each of us has two tokens. Lights add, and colours taken away. We will guess which kind of mixing each card shows, and what colour you get.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Each player takes two tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Add or Take Away. You set up the cards and the tokens.

flow.do: Play the first three cards slowly. After each card, read the back aloud and talk about it before moving on.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Everyone chooses a token. Turn them over together. Now the reader reads the back. Who chose right? Who can say why?
flow.kid: The reader reads a card. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: What do the cards in the lights-add group have in common?
good: Light from more than one place lands on the same spot.
The mix gets brighter, not darker.
There are torches, lamps or screens.

check.q: Red cellophane and green cellophane are held together in front of a torch. Which kind of mixing is that?
options: Lights add
Colours taken away
Neither
check.why: Two sheets in front of one torch each take colours away from the same beam. The light that gets through both is dim. Choosing 'lights add' is common, because two colours are involved. But here only one light shines, and the sheets only remove colours.

flow.context: In this step, you play three practice cards and learn how to score.

flow.do: Play the next cards until you have played about twelve. The reader reads the back each time. Keep a tally of points on paper.
flow.say: Your turn to guess. Choose your token and think of your colour. Turn them over together. Then listen to the back and keep your score.
flow.kid: Read the card. Pick a token. Think of a colour. Turn it over. Score a point.
flow.parent: Younger players can name just the token. Older players can name the colour as well. Accept a close name, such as blue-green for cyan. If a card has a surprising answer, such as yellow and blue dots giving a greyish colour, stop and talk about it. It follows the lights-add rule, because dots blend in the eye.

check.q: A card says a red torch and a blue torch shine on one spot of a white wall. What should you guess?
options: Lights add, and the spot looks magenta
Colours taken away, and the spot looks purple
Lights add, and the spot looks yellow
check.why: Two torches add their light on the same spot, and red plus blue makes magenta, a bright pink-purple. Choosing 'taken away' mixes up torches with paints. Choosing yellow is a mix-up with red plus green.

flow.context: In this step, you play most of the game and keep score.

flow.do: Play the last cards. Count the points. Find out who won.
flow.say: Last cards! Then count your points. Who won?
flow.kid: Play the last cards. Count your points.
flow.context: In this step, you finish the game and count the points.

flow.do: Sit together and ask the question below. Do not give the answer. Let each person say what they think.
flow.say: Look back at the cards. Why do lights make things brighter and paints make things darker?
flow.kid: Why do lights get brighter when mixed? Why do paints get darker?
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. Each torch sends new light to the spot, so there is more of it. Each paint or filter takes some light away before it reaches your eye, so there is less of it.
flow.think: Lights add light to the spot. Paints and filters take light away. Is there a mix that adds and takes away at the same time?
flow.context: This is the last step of Add or Take Away. You think about what the two kinds of mixing have in common.

items.p: A red torch and a green torch shine on the same spot of a white wall. What colour does the spot look?
items.why: Each torch adds its light to the spot. Red plus green looks yellow. Picking 'brown' is common, because red paint and green paint make brown. But torches add light, and paints take light away.

items.p: A green torch and a blue torch shine on one spot of a white wall. What colour does the spot look?
items.why: Green plus blue makes cyan, a bright blue-green. Yellow is made by red plus green, and magenta is made by red plus blue.

items.p: Red light and blue light shining together make a bright pink-purple called ____.
items.why: Red plus blue light, with no green, makes magenta. It is not in the rainbow. Your eyes and brain make it.

items.p: When you mix coloured lights, the mix is brighter than each light alone.
items.why: True. Each light adds more light to the spot. This is why red, green and blue lights together make white.

items.p: Red cellophane over a torch adds red light to the beam.
items.why: False. The cellophane makes no light. It only lets the red part of the light through and takes the other colours away.

items.p: A teacher says that mixing more and more paints always makes a darker colour. Which sentence best explains why?
opts: Each paint takes some colours of light away, so less light comes back
Paints are made of darker stuff than light
Paint is heavy, so it sinks the colour
items.why: Each paint takes some colours out of the light that falls on it. Mixing many paints takes away many colours, so little light comes back. Picking 'heavy' mixes up paint with weight. Colour is about light.

items.p: Sort these. Does each one show lights adding together, or colours being taken away?
items: a red lamp and a blue lamp lighting one curtain
a yellow highlighter over a blue one
stirring all the paints into one pot
items.a: see items
items.why: Lamps and screens send out light, and the lights add up. Cellophane, highlighters and paints do not make light. They take colours away from the light that falls on them.

items.p: Match each mix of lights to the colour it makes on a white wall.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: The three primary colours of light add up to make the other colours, and all three together make white.

items.p: In the Two Torches test, one shadow of the pencil was green, not black. Explain in two or three sentences why it was green.
items.a: The pencil blocked the red torch at that spot. The green torch's light still reached it. So the shadow was lit by green light only, and it looked green.
items.why: A strong answer says that a shadow is only dark where all the light is blocked. Where just one light is blocked, the other light still lands there.

items.p: A green leaf is held under a pure red light. What does the leaf look like?
items.why: The leaf sends back only green light. A pure red light has almost no green in it, so the leaf has little to send back. Picking 'bright green' forgets that a thing can only show the colours that fall on it.

items.p: A yellow cloth looks bright in red light and in green light, but dark in ____ light.
items.why: Yellow cloth sends back red and green, and takes away blue. In blue light it has almost nothing to send back.

items.p: Colour printers use cyan, magenta and yellow ink, and one more. Which one?
items.why: Mixing all three inks gives a dark muddy colour, not a true black. Black ink makes dark lines and shadows sharp. White comes from the paper.

items.p: Draw a red torch and a green torch shining on a white wall. Show where the wall looks red, where it looks green and where it looks yellow.
items.a: The red torch lights one round patch red. The green torch lights another patch green. Where the two patches overlap, the wall looks yellow.
items.why: Each torch lights its own patch. Only where both reach does the wall add the colours together.
items.art: A blank page with a rectangle for a wall and two torch outlines on the left and right.

items.p: Put these three stage looks in order, from the least light on the stage to the most.
items: Red, green and blue lamps all on
items.a: order shown
items.why: Each lamp adds more light. One lamp gives the least, two give more, and three give the most. All three together look white.

items.p: From far away, a square of thin red and green stripes looks yellowish-brown. Where does the mixing happen?
items.why: The stripes never mix on the paper. From far away, their light lands on the same cone cells in your eye and adds up there.

items.p: A friend says, 'Red and green make brown, because that is what paints do.' Write two sentences to help your friend. What is different about lights?
items.a: Paints take colours away from the light, so mixing them makes things darker and browner. Lights add colours, so red and green lights together make yellow, which is brighter.
items.why: A strong answer says the two kinds of mixing do opposite things: paints take away and lights add.

items.p: A phone screen can show a bright yellow, but it has no yellow dots. How does it do it?
opts: It lights its red and green dots together
It uses a special yellow filter
It turns the blue dots black
items.why: Red and green light together look yellow to your eyes. A screen only needs red, green and blue dots to show nearly every colour.

items.p: Cyan paint sends back green and blue light and takes away red. Yellow paint sends back red and green and takes away blue. Mixed together, which colour do both paints send back?
items.why: Green is the only colour that both paints send back. Red is taken away by the cyan, and blue is taken away by the yellow. So the mix looks green.

items.p: Why do colour printers add black ink to cyan, magenta and yellow?
opts: The three together make a muddy dark colour, not a deep black
Black ink is cheaper than the other colours
Black is a primary colour of paint
items.why: Cyan, magenta and yellow together take away most light, but not all. The result is a dark brownish grey. A separate black ink gives a true black and sharp letters.

items.p: A screen with red, green and blue dots can show every colour that the human eye can see.
items.why: False. Screens show a very large range of colours, but a pure green or blue-green, like the light of a laser, is stronger than any screen can make.

items.p: After staring at a green shape and looking at a white wall, you may see a pink ghost. This is called an ____.
items.why: An afterimage is made in your eye. The cone cells that sensed green tired, so white looks a little pink for a moment.

items.p: You stare at a red square, then look at a white wall and see a faint blue-green square. Where is that blue-green square?
opts: Only in your eyes and brain
items.why: The wall is plain white. The ghost square is made by tired cone cells in your eye. If you look at a different wall, it follows your eyes.

items.p: Sort these. Seen through red cellophane, does each ink on white paper seem to vanish, or look dark?
items.a: see items
items.why: Red cellophane lets only red light through. The white paper, the red ink and the yellow ink all send back plenty of red, so they look alike. Green, blue and black inks send back almost no red, so they look dark.

items.p: Match each filter to the colours of light that it lets through.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: A filter lets through its own colours and takes the rest away. Cyan is green plus blue, yellow is red plus green, and magenta is red plus blue.

items.p: Explain why red cellophane and green cellophane held together in front of a torch let almost no light through.
items.a: The red cellophane lets red light through and takes away the other colours, including green. The green cellophane then takes away the red light that got through. So almost no light gets past both sheets.
items.why: A strong answer follows the light through the first sheet and then the second. It says what each sheet lets through and what it takes away.

items.p: A navy cloth and a black cloth look alike under a warm yellowish bulb. Where would be the best place to tell them apart?
items.why: Daylight holds plenty of blue light, so the navy cloth has blue to send back and looks clearly blue. A warm bulb gives out little blue.

items.p: Draw a red, a green and a blue torch shining on one spot of a white wall. Label the colour in the middle. Label the colour where just two beams overlap.
items.a: The three beams overlap in the middle, which looks white. Red and green overlap as yellow. Green and blue overlap as cyan. Red and blue overlap as magenta.
items.why: Each pair of lights makes a secondary colour, and all three together make white.
items.art: A blank page with a wall rectangle and three torch outlines pointing at it.

items.p: Is yellow in the light, or in us? People disagree.

views.says: Yellow light is light of one wavelength. Red plus green is a different mix that happens to fool our eyes. The yellow is in the light.
Colour is what the eye and brain make. The same cone signals make the same yellow, whatever the light was. The yellow is made in us.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with? Use what you saw in the Two Torches test as evidence. Then say what the other view has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and uses evidence. For example: the wall looked yellow with no yellow light, so the yellow was made by the eye. Or: the torches were different from real yellow, so a machine could tell the difference. It then gives the other side a fair point.
items.why: Both are right about different things. Physicists measure the light, and vision scientists study the experience. How we name a colour depends on both.

items.p: Tiny dots of yellow and blue ink, seen from far away, blend into green.
items.why: False. From far away, the light from the dots adds up in your eye and looks pale and greyish. Green appears only when yellow and blue are mixed as paints, one over the other.

items.p: A cloth looks maroon in the shop and a brownish red at home. Give two reasons why its colour might look different.
items.a: The lamps in the shop and the light at home are not the same mix of colours, so the cloth has different light to send back. Also, my brain may adjust for the light differently in a bright shop and a dim room.
items.why: A strong answer gives two reasons: the light is different, and the brain's adjustment is different. Colour depends on the light as well as on the cloth.

items.p: A mix of red and green light looks the same as pure yellow light to your eyes. What does this tell us?
opts: Our eyes cannot tell apart different mixes that give the same three signals
Red and green light are really yellow
items.why: Your eyes only report three signals. Different mixes of light can give the same three signals, and then they look the same to us.

items.p: Which is the odd one out? Yellow and blue paint stirred together, a yellow sheet over a cyan sheet, two highlighters crossing, red and green torches on a wall. Say why.
items.a: red and green torches on a wall
items.why: The torches add light together. The other three take colours away from the light, so they get darker. Only the torches get brighter.

items.p: A green leaf and a yellow flower are put under the same blue light. Which one looks brighter? Say why.
items.a: Both look dark. The leaf sends back green and the flower sends back red and green, and a blue light has almost none of either. Both have little to send back, so both look dark.
items.why: A strong answer says that a thing can only send back colours that fall on it. A blue light has almost no red or green.

items.p: A scientist looks at a yellow lamp and at a screen showing yellow through an instrument that spreads light by wavelength. What does she find?
opts: Different wavelengths, even though they look alike
items.why: The yellow lamp has light of one yellow wavelength. The screen has a red wavelength and a green wavelength, but no yellow. Our eyes cannot tell them apart, but the instrument can.

items.p: Thomas Young guessed in 1802 that the eye has only three kinds of detector. Name two things you saw or did in this unit that fit his guess.
items.a: Red and green torches made a yellow wall, so two lights could stand in for one colour. Phone screens show every colour with only red, green and blue dots. If the eye had a separate detector for yellow, red plus green might not look yellow.
items.why: A strong answer gives two pieces of evidence and says how each one fits the idea of three detectors.

items.p: A dog has two kinds of cone cell. Which statement fits best?
opts: Some colours that differ to us may look alike to a dog
A dog sees only black and white
A dog sees more colours than we do
items.why: Tests on dogs suggest they tell blue and yellow apart, but mix up red and green. With two signals instead of three, fewer kinds of difference can be told apart.

items.p: Many birds have four kinds of cone cell. What could this let a bird do?
opts: Tell apart some mixes of light that look the same to us
items.why: A fourth kind gives a fourth signal to compare, so a bird can notice differences that give us the same three signals. Birds also see some ultraviolet.

items.p: A person with red-green colour blindness cannot see any colours.
items.why: False. Most people with red-green colour blindness see many colours. They mix up some reds and greens, because one of their three kinds of cone cell works differently.

items.p: In 1861, a picture of a tartan ribbon was made from three black and white photographs, each taken through a red, a green or a blue ____.
items.why: Each photograph recorded how much of one colour was in the ribbon. Shone back through the same filters on one screen, they made a colour picture.

items.p: Georges Seurat painted with small dots of pure colour instead of mixing paints. Why might a painter choose dots?
items.a: From a distance, the dots mix in the eye by adding light, so the colours look brighter than the same paints mixed together. Mixed paints get darker because each takes away colours.
items.why: A strong answer says that optical mixing adds light, while mixing paint takes colours away. Dots can keep colours brighter.

items.p: Sort these. Do scientists agree on it, or does nobody know yet?
items: Red and green light together look yellow.
Filters take colours away from white light.
Most people have three kinds of cone cell.
What yellow feels like inside another person.
Exactly how the brain turns cone signals into the feeling of a colour.
items.a: see items
items.why: The first three have been tested many times. What colour feels like from the inside, and how signals become a feeling, are still open questions.

items.p: A stage designer has red, green and blue lamps. She wants a pale pink glow. Which plan is best?
opts: A strong red lamp with weaker green and blue lamps
items.why: Pink is red mixed with a little white. A strong red with weaker green and blue adds the white to the red. Only blue or only green would not give any red.

items.p: Plan a fair test to find out whether the distance of the torches from the wall changes the colour made by a red torch and a green torch. Say what you change, what you keep the same, and what you look for.
items.a: I change the distance of the green torch from the wall: 50 centimetres, 1 metre and 2 metres. I keep the red torch, the wall, the room and the cellophane the same. I look at the colour of the overlap each time and write it down. I try each distance twice.
items.why: A strong answer changes only one thing, keeps the rest the same, repeats the test and says what it will look at. A fainter green torch should make the overlap look more orange.

items.p: What are the three primary colours? People give different answers.

views.says: Red, yellow and blue. You can mix many paints from these.
Cyan, magenta and yellow. These make the widest range of colours from ink.
Red, green and blue. These are the three lights that make nearly every colour on a screen.

items.ask: Whose answer is best? Use two things you did in this unit as evidence. Then say when another answer would be better.
items.a: A strong answer says that the right set depends on whether you are mixing light or taking colours away. It uses the torch test and the highlighter test as evidence.
items.why: There is no single set of basic colours for everything. For lights, red, green and blue work best. For inks, cyan, magenta and yellow work best.

items.p: Many people looked at the same photo of a dress and saw different colours. What best explains it?
opts: Their brains guessed different colours for the light that fell on the dress
Some people have no cone cells
items.why: The brain tries to remove the colour of the light to find the true colour of a thing. In a photo with unclear light, brains can guess differently.

items.p: A TV looks like a smooth picture from the sofa, but like separate coloured dots from one centimetre away. Why?
opts: From far away, the dots are too small and close for the eye to tell apart, so their light blends
The dots move apart when you step back
The TV changes its picture when you come near
items.why: Your eye can only tell dots apart if they are far enough apart. Further away, their light lands on the same cone cells and adds up.

items.p: Draw a white wall lit by a red torch on the left and a blue torch on the right, with a pencil in front. Colour the lit wall and the two shadows.
items.a: The middle where both lights reach looks magenta. The shadow where the red light is blocked looks blue. The shadow where the blue light is blocked looks red.
items.why: Each shadow takes the colour of the light that still reaches it.
items.art: A blank page with a wall rectangle, a pencil in front, and a red torch and a blue torch outlined at each side.

items.p: Label the drawing of the back of an eye. Show a cone cell that responds best to red, one to green and one to blue, and the nerve to the brain.
items.a: Three kinds of cone cells lie in the retina. They are labelled red, green and blue, and a nerve leaves the eye towards the brain.
items.why: The brain compares the signals from the three kinds of cone cell and builds the colour we see.
items.art: A simple drawing of the back of an eye with three kinds of cone cells in the retina and a nerve leaving it.

items.p: Put these in order from the fewest kinds of cone cell to the most.
items: A person with usual colour vision
items.a: order shown
items.why: A dog usually has two kinds of cone cell. Most people have three. Many birds have four.

experiments.title: Two Torches, Two Shadows: what colour is a shadow?
experiments.question: When a red torch and a green torch shine on one white wall, what colour is the wall where they overlap? And what colour is each shadow of a pencil in front of the wall?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. What colour will the wall be where the red and green lights overlap? What colour will the pencil's shadows be? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same two torches, the same wall, the same pencil and the same dim room each time. Keep both torches between half a metre and one metre from the wall, and move them closer if the patches look faint. Change one thing at a time: first only red, then only green, then both. Look at each set-up for a full ten seconds, because your eyes need time to settle in a dim room. Safety: use LED or phone torches, because cellophane can melt on a hot bulb, and never shine a torch into anyone's eyes. Who does what: with one child, the child holds the red torch and the parent holds the green. With 2 to 4 children, one holds each torch, one holds the pencil and one is the recorder with the table. Swap jobs for each set-up. If you have only one phone, use a small LED torch for the second light.
results_table: Colour of the wall where the light lands
Was my guess right? (yes or no)

materials.item: 2 small LED torches or phone torches (LED, not a hot bulb)
red cellophane and green cellophane, each big enough to fold into two layers over a torch (gift wrap, or see-through sweet wrappers)
rubber bands or tape to hold the cellophane on
a pencil, or better a thick marker pen, standing upright in a lump of clay or dough (a thick shadow is easier to see)
a plain white wall, or a big sheet of white card taped to a wall
a room you can make dim: curtains closed in the evening, or at night with the other lights off (daylight washes the colours out)
blue cellophane, and a third torch to put it on, if you have them (optional)
a pencil and the results table

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the wall and the pencil's two shadows with coloured pencils. Write what you thought, what you saw and why.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you shine a red torch and a green torch on a white wall. You find out what colour the two lights make together, and what colour the shadows are.

setup.art: A torch with red cellophane held on by a rubber band, and a second torch with green cellophane, side by side on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Fix red cellophane on one torch and green cellophane on the other.

setup.art: A pencil standing in a lump of clay in front of a white wall, with the red torch alone shining and a single dark red shadow.
setup.caption: 2. Stand a pencil near the wall. Shine the red torch alone.

setup.art: The same pencil lit by the green torch alone, with a single dark green shadow.
setup.caption: 3. Shine the green torch alone.

setup.art: Both torches shining so that a red patch and a green patch overlap into a yellow patch, with one red shadow and one green shadow of the pencil.
setup.caption: 4. Shine both torches so the two patches overlap. Look at the middle and at the shadows.

setup.art: A third torch with blue cellophane added, with a white middle patch and three shadows of cyan, magenta and yellow.
setup.caption: 5. If you have a blue torch, add it. Write the colours in your table.

flow.do: Show your child the two torches, the cellophane and the white wall. Ask for a guess and a reason for each question. Write the guesses at the top of the table.
flow.say: We will cover one torch with red and one with green. Then we shine both on the wall. What colour will the wall be where the two lights meet? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A red torch and a green torch. Both shine on one wall. What colour will it be? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think the wall will be that colour?
good: Red and green paint make brown, so it might be brown.
It might look like a colour from the middle of the rainbow.

ask.q: What colour will the pencil's shadows be?
good: Black or grey, like all shadows.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children guess brown, because they know paints. That is a good guess, and the test will show if it holds. Write what they say, word for word.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Two Torches test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Fold the red cellophane in two. Fix it over the front of one torch with a rubber band. Do the same with the green cellophane on the other torch. Dim the room. Shine each torch alone on the wall.
flow.say: Cover each torch with cellophane. Keep the sheet tight and flat. Now shine each torch alone on the wall. What colour is each patch?
flow.kid: Fix red on one torch. Fix green on the other. Shine each on the wall. What colours do you see?
flow.parent: Dim the room by closing the curtains, ideally in the evening. If a patch is very faint, use one layer of cellophane, or move the torch closer to the wall. If a patch looks pale, add a second layer. Cheap cellophane lets a little white light through, so a patch can look slightly pale. That is fine.

check.q: Why do we shine each torch alone on the wall before using both together?
options: So we know what each light does alone, and can tell what is new when we use both
So that the torches do not use up their batteries
Because the wall needs time to warm up
check.why: In a fair test you first see each thing alone. Then you can tell what changes when you put them together. Picking 'batteries' or 'the wall warms up' gives a reason that has nothing to do with colour.

flow.context: In this step, you make the two coloured torches and test each one alone.

flow.do: Stand the pencil upright in the clay, a hand's width from the wall. Switch on the red torch alone from about one metre away. Look at the shadow. Then switch on the green torch alone and look again.
flow.say: Here is the pencil. First only the red torch. What colour is the shadow? Now only the green. What colour is the shadow now?
flow.kid: Stand the pencil near the wall. Shine the red torch. Look at the shadow. Now shine the green. Look again.
flow.parent: With one torch, the shadow is dark, and the rest of the wall is the colour of the torch. The shadow may look dark red, dark green or almost black. Write what you really see. If the pencil's shadow is too thin to see, use a thick marker pen instead. This is your starting point for the next step.
flow.context: In this step, you see the shadow of a pencil with only one light at a time.

flow.do: Switch on both torches. Stand them about 40 centimetres apart and about one metre from the wall, so the two patches overlap. Look at the middle. Then look at the pencil's two shadows. Write the colours in the table. Then move one torch back a hand-span at a time, and write how the middle colour changes each time.
flow.say: Both torches now, side by side, so the patches overlap. What colour is the wall in the middle? How many shadows does the pencil have? What colour is each one?
flow.kid: Switch on both torches. Make the patches overlap. What colour is the middle? What colour is each shadow?

ask.q: What do you notice about the shadows?
good: One shadow is red and one is green.
The shadows are not black or grey.

flow.parent: Expect the overlap to look yellow, or orange-yellow, or sometimes pale green-yellow, depending on which torch is stronger. If it looks orange, the red is too strong, so move the red torch a little further back. If it looks green-yellow, move the green torch back. One shadow should look green and the other red. The shadows can be faint, so a darker room helps. The yellow will not be perfect. That is a real result.

check.q: One of the pencil's shadows is green. Why?
options: The pencil blocks the red torch there, but the green torch still lights that spot
The pencil is painted green
The green torch is brighter than the red torch
check.why: A shadow is a place where one light is blocked. Where the red torch is blocked, the green torch still reaches the wall, so that shadow looks green. Picking 'painted green' cannot be right, because the other shadow is red. Picking 'brighter' does not explain why one shadow is green and the other red.

chart.title: Made-up example: how a filled-in table can look

flow.context: In this step, you shine both torches at once and look at the overlap and the two shadows.

flow.do: If you have a third torch, cover it with blue cellophane. Switch on all three so the patches overlap. Look at the middle and at the pencil's three shadows. With only two torches, swap the green one for blue and see what red and blue make.
flow.say: Now a third torch, with blue. Where all three meet, what colour is the wall? What colours are the three shadows?
flow.kid: Add a blue torch. What colour is the middle? What colours are the shadows?
flow.parent: Blue cellophane is dim, so use only one layer of blue and move the blue torch closer. Expect the middle to look white or pale. The three shadows should look cyan, magenta and yellow. With only two torches, red and blue give magenta. Green and blue give cyan. This step is a bonus. Skip it if your torches are weak.
flow.context: In this step, you add a blue torch, or swap the green for blue, and look at the new colours.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now about mixing lights? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: red light and green light together look yellow. What I saw: the wall was yellow where the two patches overlapped, and the pencil had one red shadow and one green shadow. Why: each torch adds its light to the spot, and the eye gives the same answer to red plus green as it does to yellow.
flow.context: In this step, you finish like a scientist, with claim, evidence and reasoning.

experiments.title: Highlighter Layers: do inks add colours or take them away?
experiments.question: When you colour one highlighter over another on white paper, do the colours add up like torch light, or do they take colours away?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. What colour will yellow over blue be? What colour will pink over yellow be? Will the crossing look brighter or darker than the single colours? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same three highlighters and the same kind of white paper every time. Colour each stripe with one slow stroke and the same pressure. Only the colours you put on top of each other change. At the end, check whether the order of the layers matters.
results_table: Lighter or darker than the single colours?

materials.item: 3 highlighters: a yellow, a pink and a blue (a blue-green one is fine). A light blue or turquoise sketch pen can stand in for the blue, but its layers will look weaker.
2 sheets of plain white paper
a ruler
coloured pencils to record the colours
a pencil and the results table
a window or a lamp to look by

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the nine crossing squares and colour each one in with coloured pencils. Write which crossings are darker than the single stripes.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you draw highlighter stripes across each other on white paper. You find out what colours the crossings make, and whether they are lighter or darker than the stripes.

setup.art: A white page with three wide horizontal highlighter stripes, yellow, pink and blue, one under another, with gaps between them.
setup.caption: 1. Draw three wide stripes across the page, in yellow, pink and blue.

setup.art: The same page with three tall highlighter stripes crossing the first three, forming a grid of nine squares.
setup.caption: 2. Draw three tall stripes down the page, in blue, yellow and pink, crossing the first ones.

setup.art: A close-up of the grid with the crossing squares coloured: green, orange-red, purple and deeper versions of each stripe colour.
setup.caption: 3. Look at the nine crossings. Write the colour of each in your table.

setup.art: A short diagonal stripe in the third colour drawn over one crossing, making a dark patch, and a second small patch with two colours in the opposite order.
setup.caption: 4. Test all three layers together, and test the opposite order.

flow.do: Show your child the three highlighters and the paper. Ask for a guess and a reason for each question. Write the guesses at the top of the table.
flow.say: We will colour stripes across each other. What colour will yellow over blue be? What about pink over yellow? Will the crossings be brighter or darker? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three highlighters. We will draw stripes across each other. What colours will the crossings be? Why?

ask.q: Will the crossings look brighter or darker than the single stripes?

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Children who have just done the torch test often guess brighter. Others who know paints guess darker. Both are good guesses. Write what they say.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Highlighter Layers test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Use the ruler to draw three wide horizontal stripes across the first page: yellow, pink and blue. Leave a gap of one finger-width between them. Colour each with one slow stroke. Close each cap after use. Keep the pens away from your mouth and eyes.
flow.say: Draw three stripes across the page. Yellow, then pink, then blue. One slow stroke each. Leave a gap between them.
flow.kid: Draw three stripes across. Yellow, pink, blue. Leave gaps.
flow.context: In this step, you draw the first three stripes of the grid.
flow.parent: Use plain printer or copy paper, because highlighter ink bleeds through thin paper. Try each pen on a scrap first. One child: the parent can draw a second grid with the same pens, to compare. 2 to 4 children: share the three pens and pass them round, so each child draws a grid on their own page. Then compare grids. Do different hands give different colours?

flow.do: Now draw three tall stripes down the page, from top to bottom, crossing the first ones. Use blue first, then yellow, then pink. Leave gaps between them. Use the same pressure each time.
flow.say: Now three tall stripes, crossing the first ones. Blue, yellow, pink. Same slow stroke as before.
flow.kid: Draw three tall stripes down the page. Blue, yellow, pink. Cross the first ones.
flow.parent: Wait a few seconds for the ink to dry before you look closely. The crossings of stripes of the same colour should look deeper than the single stripe. The crossings of different colours are the new ones.
flow.context: In this step, you draw the second set of stripes, which cross the first set and make nine crossing squares.

flow.do: Look at the nine crossing squares in daylight or under a lamp. Colour each square in your table and write whether it is lighter or darker than the two single stripes.
flow.say: Look at each crossing. What colour is it? Is it brighter than the stripes, or darker?
flow.kid: Look at the nine crossings. What colours do you see? Brighter or darker?

ask.q: What do you notice about the crossings of two different colours?
good: They are new colours, like green or orange.
