They are darker than the stripes.

flow.parent: Expect yellow with blue to make green. Pink with yellow makes orange or orange-red. Pink with blue makes purple or violet. Crossings of the same colour look deeper. Your highlighters may give slightly different colours from these. Write what you really see. Yellow, pink and blue are close to the three inks used in colour printers, which are yellow, magenta and cyan.

check.q: Where two different highlighter stripes cross, the square is darker than both stripes. Why?
options: Each ink takes some colours of light away, so less light comes back from the crossing
The paper is thicker at the crossing
Highlighter ink adds light, like a torch does
check.why: White light goes through the top ink and the bottom ink, bounces off the paper and goes back through both. Each ink takes colours away, so less light reaches your eye. Picking 'adds light, like a torch' is the common mix-up. A torch is a light source. Ink only changes light that comes from somewhere else.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in one row of the table

flow.context: In this step, you look at the crossings and write down what you see.

flow.do: On the second sheet, colour a short yellow stripe. Colour a blue stripe across it. Then colour a pink stripe across the crossing. Look at the colour where all three layers meet. Then colour one patch with blue first and yellow second, and compare it with yellow first and blue second. Last, colour a yellow patch with one stroke, then two, then three. Write how the colour changes.
flow.say: Three layers now. What colour is the middle where all three meet? Then try blue first and yellow second. Is it the same green?
flow.kid: Put all three colours on top of each other. What colour is it? Does the order change anything?
flow.parent: Three layers usually give a dark brownish or greyish colour. The order often makes only a small difference. If you see a small difference, write it down as a real result. Different inks soak in at different rates.
flow.context: In this step, you test all three layers together and test whether the order of the layers matters.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now about mixing inks? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: inks take colours away, so mixing them makes the colour darker. What I saw: yellow over blue made a darker green, and all three layers made a dark colour. Why: each ink takes some colours out of the light, so less light comes back to my eye.
flow.context: In this step, you finish like a scientist, with claim, evidence and reasoning.

activities.title: The Wrong-Colour Flag: afterimages in your eyes

materials.item: a sheet of plain white paper
felt pens: a bold blue-green (cyan, turquoise, sky blue or sea-green), a black and a pink (magenta)
a ruler and a pencil
a bright lamp or a sunny window
a plain white wall, or a clean white page, to look at afterwards
a clock or phone timer

schedule.what: Draw the flag in the wrong colours. Stare at it. Look at a white wall and see what appears.

activities.record: Draw the flag you drew, and next to it draw the flag you saw on the white wall. Colour both. Write how long the ghost flag lasted.
activities.context: In this activity, you draw a flag in colours that are not the real ones. You stare at it, and then look at a white wall. Your eyes show you the real colours.

setup.art: A white page with a rectangle divided into three stripes: top blue-green, middle black with a small white dot in it, bottom pink.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the flag in the wrong colours. Leave a white dot in the middle.

setup.art: A child staring at the white dot under a bright lamp, with a clock showing thirty seconds.
setup.caption: 2. Stare at the white dot for thirty seconds without moving your eyes.

setup.art: The child looking at a white wall where a faint orange, white and green flag floats.
setup.caption: 3. Look at the white wall. What appears?

flow.do: Draw a rectangle 12 centimetres wide and 9 centimetres tall. Divide it into three stripes. Colour the top stripe blue-green, the middle stripe black and the bottom stripe pink. Leave a small round spot in the middle uncoloured.
flow.say: We will draw India's flag in the wrong colours. Top is blue-green. Middle is black. Bottom is pink. In the middle, leave a little white dot to stare at. What colours do you think you will see on a white wall afterwards?
flow.kid: Draw three stripes. Top blue-green. Middle black. Bottom pink. Leave a white dot in the middle.

ask.q: What colours do you think you will see on the white wall after staring?
good: The same colours as the flag.

flow.parent: The real flag has saffron on top, white in the middle and green at the bottom. Do not say this yet. Let your child guess first. Colour the stripes boldly, so the colours are strong.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Wrong-Colour Flag. You draw the flag, and you guess before you test.

flow.do: Put the flag under a bright lamp or in a sunny window. Look at the white dot in the middle. Count slowly to 30 without moving your eyes. Then look at a plain white wall, and keep your eyes still. Blink once.
flow.say: Stare at the white dot. Count slowly to thirty. Do not move your eyes. Now look at the white wall. What do you see?
flow.kid: Stare at the white dot. Count to thirty. Do not move your eyes. Then look at the white wall.
flow.parent: Expect a faint ghost flag with a reddish-orange top, a whitish middle and a greenish bottom, for a few seconds. It fades fast. If nothing appears, stare for 45 seconds under a brighter light, and look at a plain white wall, not a textured one. Some people see it clearly and others only faintly. Both are normal. Rest your eyes for a minute between tries. Safety: stare only at the paper, never at the Sun or at a bare bulb.

check.q: The top stripe was blue-green. On the white wall you saw a faint orange-red stripe there. Where was the orange-red made?
options: In your eye, because the cone cells that sensed blue-green had grown tired
On the wall, where there was a secret colour
In the felt pen, which dried slowly
check.why: The orange-red was made in your eyes. The cone cells that respond to blue-green worked hard while you stared, and they tired. Looking at white, they answered less than usual. The other cones answered as normal, so the white looked a little red. Picking 'on the wall' is natural, but the wall is plain white. Look at another wall and the ghost moves with your eyes.

flow.context: In this step, you stare at the flag and then look at a white wall.

flow.do: Ask another person to try the same test, while you watch. Ask them to say what they see. Compare what they say with what you saw. With 2 to 4 children, everyone tries it at the same time and calls out how many seconds their ghost flag lasts. Write the times down and compare.
flow.say: Now let someone else try. Do they see the same flag? Are the colours the same as yours?
flow.kid: Ask someone else to try. Do they see the same flag?
flow.parent: People differ. Some see a clear tricolour, some see faint patches. That tells us that afterimages depend on the eye that makes them. Draw both flags if you can.
flow.context: In this step, you ask another person to try the test and compare what you both saw.

flow.do: Now draw a large red square on a new page, with a white dot in the middle. Ask your child to guess the colour of the ghost square. Then stare at it for 30 seconds and look at the white wall.
flow.say: One more. Guess first. If you stare at a red square, what colour is the ghost on the white wall? Then try.
flow.kid: Draw a red square. Guess the ghost colour. Stare. Look at the white wall.
flow.parent: Expect a pale blue-green ghost. The ghost of green is pink. The ghost of yellow is blue. These pairs are called complementary colours. They are not the same as the colours of the wall. They are made in the eye.
flow.think: The ghost of red was blue-green, and the ghost of blue-green was red. What do you notice about the pairs?
flow.context: In this step, you predict and test the afterimage of a red square.

activities.title: Stripes That Blend: colours that mix in your eye

materials.item: a sheet of plain white paper
fine felt pens: red, green, blue and yellow
a ruler and a pencil
a colour photo from a newspaper or magazine
a magnifying glass, if you have one (a phone camera zoomed in works too)
a corridor, a long room or a terrace where you can walk away about 8 big steps

schedule.what: Draw two squares of fine stripes. Walk away until the stripes blend. Look at a newspaper photo up close.

activities.record: Fill in a small table: the stripe colours, the number of steps at which they blended, and the colour you saw from far away. Draw the colours of the dots you found in the newspaper photo.
activities.context: In this activity, you draw squares of thin coloured stripes and walk away from them. You find out where the stripes blend into one colour, and then look at the dots in a printed photo.

setup.art: Two small squares drawn on white paper, one with thin red and green stripes side by side, and one with thin blue and yellow stripes.
setup.caption: 1. Draw two squares of thin stripes, in pairs of colours.

setup.art: A child walking away from the paper held on a wall, stopping when the stripes become one smooth colour.
setup.caption: 2. Walk away until the stripes blend. Count the steps.

setup.art: A newspaper photo with a magnified circle showing small dots of cyan, magenta, yellow and black.
setup.caption: 3. Look at a printed photo through a magnifier.

flow.do: Draw two squares, each 3 centimetres wide and 3 centimetres tall. In the first, draw thin stripes side by side. Go red, green, red, green, with no gaps, until the square is full. In the second, do the same with blue and yellow.
flow.say: Draw two small squares. Fill the first with thin stripes of red and green, side by side. Fill the second with blue and yellow. Use the thin tip of the pen and no gaps.
flow.kid: Draw two squares. Fill one with thin red and green stripes. Fill one with blue and yellow.

ask.q: What colour do you think each square will look from far away?
good: Red and green might look brown.
Red and green might look yellow.
Blue and yellow might look green.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children guess green for blue and yellow, as for paint. Write their guess. The stripes should be thin, about as thin as the pen's tip, so the pen's width sets the size.
flow.context: This is the first step of Stripes That Blend. You draw the two squares.

flow.do: Stick the paper on a wall at eye height. Stand close, at about 30 centimetres. Look at the stripes. Say what you see. Then take one big step back and look again. Keep stepping back one step at a time.
flow.say: Stand close and look at the stripes. Now step back, one step at a time. Look after each step. When do the stripes stop being stripes?
flow.kid: Look at the stripes up close. Step back one step at a time. When do they blend?
flow.parent: Fine pen stripes usually blend between 2 and 8 big steps away (thicker pens need more steps), depending on your eyes and the pens. If the room is short, use a corridor or a terrace, or squint, which blurs the stripes sooner. Eyes differ, so with 2 to 4 children each child stands where they think the stripes blend and the others mark the spot with a shoe. Compare. With one child, the parent does the same test. If the stripes never blend, they are too wide. Draw thinner ones.
flow.context: In this step, you start walking away from the stripes and look after every step.

flow.do: Find the number of steps at which each square becomes one smooth colour. Write the number and the colour you see in the table. Do it for both squares.
flow.say: Stop at the step where the stripes disappear. How many steps is that? What colour is the square now? Do it for both squares.
flow.kid: Count the steps where the stripes vanish. What colour is each square?
flow.parent: Red and green stripes usually look a dull yellow or yellow-brown. Blue and yellow stripes usually look a pale grey or a greyish green. Felt-pen colours are not pure, so the result is duller than the lights in the torch test. Write what you really see. The mix is not green, which is the colour you would get by mixing the same two as paints.

check.q: From far away, the red and green stripes looked like a dull yellow-brown. What does this show?
options: Light from the red and green stripes lands on the same part of your eye and adds up
The pens ran out of ink
Red and green paint mix on the paper
check.why: From far away, light from the red stripes and the green stripes lands on the same cone cells. The light adds up, just as it did with the two torches, so you see a yellowish colour. Picking 'mix on the paper' is a common mix-up. The stripes never touched each other on the paper. The mixing happened in your eye.

flow.context: In this step, you write down where the stripes blended and what colour they became.

flow.do: Look closely at a colour photo in a newspaper or magazine, with a magnifying glass, or with a phone camera zoomed in. Find the small dots. Draw the colours of the dots you can find.
flow.say: Now look at a printed photo, very close. What do you see? Draw the colours of the little dots. How many different colours of dots are there?
flow.kid: Look closely at a printed photo. Draw the dots you see.
flow.parent: You should find tiny dots of cyan (blue-green), magenta (pink), yellow and black. Together these make every colour in the picture. Use a colour picture from a newspaper supplement, magazine or flyer, not a black-and-white page. Cheap printing shows the dots best. If you only see a blur, use a stronger magnifier or a bigger zoom.
flow.think: A printed photo is made of only four colours of ink. Where do all the other colours come from?
flow.context: In this step, you look at the dots that make up a printed colour photo.

activities.title: Navy or Black? Colours under different lamps

materials.item: 4 dark things of similar shades: for example a navy blue sock, a black sock, a dark green cloth and a maroon cloth
a sheet of white paper
a window with daylight
a warm yellowish light: a warm-white bulb, or a phone torch with yellow cellophane held over it in a dark room
a cool white light: a tubelight or cool-white LED bulb, or the plain phone torch in a dark room
a notebook and a pencil
a small piece of yellow cellophane (optional, to make a warm light)

schedule.what: Look at the dark things under daylight, a warm bulb and a cool bulb. Write which ones are easy or hard to tell apart.

activities.record: Fill in a table with one row for each kind of light: how easy it was to tell navy from black, and what colour the white paper looked. Write your score out of 4 for each light. Write which light was best for choosing dark clothes.
activities.context: In this activity, you look at the same dark things under different lamps. You find out when navy and black look alike, and why.

setup.art: Four dark cloths, navy, black, dark green and maroon, laid side by side on a table next to a sheet of white paper.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the dark things and the white paper.

setup.art: The same cloths in daylight by a window, with the navy clearly blue and the black clearly black.
setup.caption: 2. Look at them in daylight first.

setup.art: The same cloths under a warm yellowish lamp, with the navy and black looking almost the same.
setup.caption: 3. Look at them under a warm bulb, and then a cool bulb.

flow.do: Lay the dark things on a table. Show your child the pair of navy and black. Ask for a guess about whether it will be easy or hard to tell them apart under each light.
flow.say: Here are four dark things. Two look almost alike, the navy and the black. In which light will it be easiest to tell them apart? In which will it be hardest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Four dark things. Navy and black look alike. In which light is it hardest to tell them apart? Why?

ask.q: Which light do you think will make navy and black easiest to tell apart?
good: Daylight, because it is the brightest.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of Navy or Black. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Carry the things to a window in the daytime, away from direct sun. Look at the navy and the black side by side. Write if it is easy, hard or not possible to tell them apart. Look at the white paper and write its colour. Now close your eyes while a partner hands you the navy or the black without saying which. Say which you think it is. Do this 4 times and write your score out of 4. With 2 to 4 children, take turns to be the partner and the guesser. With one child, the parent is the partner.
flow.say: First, daylight. Can you tell the navy from the black? Which is darker? What colour is the white paper?
flow.kid: Look at the dark things in daylight. Can you tell navy from black? What colour is the paper?
flow.parent: In daylight, navy usually looks clearly blue and black looks black, so they are easy to tell apart. The white paper looks white.
flow.context: In this step, you look at the dark things in daylight.

flow.do: Take the things into a room lit only by a warm yellowish light (a warm bulb, or a phone torch with yellow cellophane held close to the things). Switch off other lights and close the curtains. Look again. Write if it is easy, hard or impossible to tell navy from black. Write the colour of the white paper. Repeat the 4-try naming test and write your score.
flow.say: Now the warm yellow bulb. Look at navy and black again. Can you still tell them apart? What colour is the white paper now?
flow.kid: Look at the dark things under the warm bulb. Can you tell navy from black?
flow.parent: Under a warm bulb, navy and black often look almost the same. The white paper looks yellowish, though your eyes may call it white after a minute. If you only have one kind of bulb, compare it with daylight. Never judge navy or black from a dim warm bulb. Safety: a regular bulb gets hot, so an adult should move the lamp and switch it off before anyone touches it. An LED bulb stays cooler.

check.q: Under the warm yellowish bulb, the navy and black looked almost the same. Why?
options: A warm bulb gives out very little blue light, and navy cloth sends back mostly blue
The navy cloth turned black
Warm bulbs are brighter than daylight
check.why: Navy cloth sends back mostly blue light. A warm bulb gives out little blue, so there is almost nothing for the navy cloth to send back. It looks nearly black. Picking 'turned black' is natural, but take it back to daylight and it is navy again. Nothing changed in the cloth.

flow.context: In this step, you look at the dark things under a warm yellowish bulb.

flow.do: Now use a cool white light: a tubelight, a cool-white LED bulb, or the plain phone torch in a dark room. Do the 4-try test again. Compare the three scores.
flow.say: Now a cool white light. Is it easy to tell navy from black here? What colour is the paper now?
flow.kid: Look under the cool white light. Can you tell navy from black?
flow.parent: Cool white light gives out more blue, so navy shows up as blue. Most homes have a cool-white bulb but no warm one. If so, make the warm light of step 3 with a phone torch and yellow cellophane. Scores are small numbers, so treat them as a clue, not proof.
flow.context: In this step, you look at the dark things under a cool white light, or a plain torch.

flow.do: Compare the three rows of the table. Ask your child: if you had to choose a school uniform colour for a child, in which light would you choose it? Why?
flow.say: Look at your table. In which light was it easiest to tell the colours apart? Why do you think a shopkeeper takes the cloth to the door?
flow.kid: Look at your table. Which light was best for telling dark colours apart?
flow.think: The cloth was the same in every light. What was different?
flow.context: In this step, you compare the lights and think about when to choose a colour.

activities.title: The Vanishing Message: red words that disappear

materials.item: a sheet of plain white paper
a red felt pen and a green felt pen
a sheet of red cellophane and a sheet of green cellophane, or see-through sweet wrappers
a bright room, or a window with daylight

schedule.what: Write a message in red and one in green. Look at them through red and green cellophane. Find out what vanishes.

activities.record: Draw the two words. Write what each looked like through the red sheet and through the green sheet.
activities.context: In this activity, you write one word in red and one in green. You look at them through coloured cellophane and find out why a red word can vanish.

setup.art: A white page with the word RED written in red felt pen and the word GREEN written in green felt pen.
setup.caption: 1. Write one word in red and one word in green.

setup.art: A child holding red cellophane over one eye, seeing the red word vanish and the green word turn nearly black.
setup.caption: 2. Look through red cellophane.

setup.art: The same child looking through green cellophane, now seeing the green word vanish and the red word turn dark.
setup.caption: 3. Look through green cellophane.

flow.do: Write the word RED in red felt pen, in big letters, on the white paper. Write the word GREEN in green felt pen below it. Ask your child to guess what each word will look like through red cellophane.
flow.say: Write RED in red, and GREEN in green. Hold the red cellophane over one eye. What do you think each word will look like? Why?
flow.kid: Write RED in red. Write GREEN in green. What will they look like through red cellophane? Why?

ask.q: What do you think will happen to the red word through red cellophane?

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Never look at the Sun through cellophane.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Vanishing Message. You write the words, and you guess.

flow.do: Hold the red cellophane over one eye, or in front of your eyes like a window. Look at both words. Then look through the green cellophane. Write down what each word looks like each time.
flow.say: Look through the red cellophane. Which word is easy to see? Which one has vanished? Now try green. What changes?
flow.kid: Look through the red sheet. Then the green. Which word vanishes each time?
flow.parent: Through the red cellophane, the red word seems to vanish into the white paper and the green word looks dark. Through the green cellophane, the green word vanishes and the red word looks dark. It is the same trick as the red torch and the green leaf. The paper can look a little pink or green through the sheet. If the red word only fades and does not vanish, use two layers of cellophane, a brighter room, or a truer red pen. Some sweet wrappers are orange, not red, and will not work as well.

check.q: Through red cellophane, the red word vanished and the green word turned dark. Why?
options: Red paper and red ink both send back plenty of red light, and green ink sends back almost none
The red cellophane painted over the red word
Green ink is darker than red ink
check.why: The red cellophane lets only red light through. The white paper sends back plenty of red, and so does the red ink, so they look the same. The green ink sends back almost no red, so it looks dark. Picking 'painted over' sounds sensible, but the word is still there. Take the cellophane away and it comes back.

flow.context: In this step, you look at the two words through red and then green cellophane.

flow.do: Write a secret message in red felt pen on white paper. Then scribble green felt-pen lines all over and around the words. Give it to a friend. Ask them to look through the green cellophane (the green scribbles fade and the red message shows dark), and then through the red cellophane (the message hides), and say what happens. With one child, the parent is the friend. With 2 to 4 children, swap messages in pairs.
flow.say: Write a short secret message to a friend, in red. Give them the green cellophane to read it with. Then the red one. What happens?
flow.kid: Write a secret in red. Read it through green. Then red. What happens?
flow.think: A message in red vanishes through red cellophane. What colour of pen would vanish through blue cellophane?
flow.context: In this step, you use the trick to make a message that only shows through one sheet.

projects.title: A Coloured Shadow Puppet Show

materials.item: a thin white cotton cloth, such as an old dupatta, bedsheet or thin pillowcase, about 1 metre square, to use as a screen (a thick cloth lets too little light through)
stiff card from an old cereal box
scraps of red, green, blue and yellow cellophane or see-through sweet wrappers
glue, tape and scissors (a grown-up cuts the windows)
3 ice-cream sticks or straws to hold the puppets
2 torches, or 2 phone torches
two chairs or a clothes line to hang the screen

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts the windows in the card, because scissors and craft knives can slip. Use LED or phone torches only, because cellophane can melt on a hot bulb.

schedule.what: Plan and draw three puppets. Cut out their windows and stick cellophane on them. Leave the glue to dry.
Hang the screen. Put on a short show with a white torch, and then with coloured torches.

projects.record: Draw one puppet. Colour its windows. Write what each window looked like in white light, in red light and in green light.
projects.context: In this project, you make card puppets with coloured windows and perform a shadow show. You find out how coloured windows look under white light and coloured light.

setup.art: A card puppet shaped like a bird with three round windows cut out, one covered with red cellophane, one with green and one with yellow.
setup.caption: 1. Cut a puppet from card. Cut windows. Stick coloured cellophane over them.

setup.art: A thin white sheet hung between two chairs, with a torch behind it and a child holding a puppet on a stick in front of the torch.
setup.caption: 2. Hang the screen. Put a torch behind the puppet.

setup.art: A bird puppet's shadow on the screen, dark, with three bright coloured windows glowing red, green and yellow.
setup.caption: 3. Look at the screen from the front. The windows glow with colour.

flow.do: Show your child the cardboard, cellophane and torches. Ask what the puppets will look like on the screen. Ask them to draw three puppet shapes on paper with windows marked in colour.
flow.say: We will make shadow puppets with coloured windows. What colour will the puppet's body be on the screen? What will the windows look like? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: We make puppets with coloured windows. What will the body look like on the screen? The windows?

ask.q: What will the puppet's body look like on the screen?
What will the windows look like?

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. In the tradition of tholu bommalata in Andhra Pradesh, puppeteers use large puppets of thin, painted leather. Light shines through the leather, and the colours appear on the screen.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Coloured Shadow Puppet Show. You plan the puppets, and you guess.

flow.do: Draw each puppet on the card. A grown-up cuts out the shape and cuts two or three windows in each, about 3 centimetres wide. Stick coloured cellophane over each window with glue or tape. Stick a puppet to a stick.
flow.say: Draw a puppet on card. Cut out the shape. Ask a grown-up to cut windows in it. Cover each window with cellophane. Stick the puppet to a stick.
flow.kid: Draw a puppet on card. A grown-up cuts it out. Cover the windows with cellophane. Add a stick.
flow.parent: A grown-up should do all the cutting. Keep the windows big, so the colour is bright on the screen. Use one colour per window. Make three puppets, so you have different colour windows to compare.
flow.context: In this step, you make the puppets and cover their windows with coloured cellophane.

flow.do: Let the glue dry until tomorrow. Meanwhile, hang the screen between two chairs or on a clothes line. Make the room dim. Try a test: hold a puppet close behind the screen and shine a torch from behind.
flow.say: While the glue dries, hang the white cloth between two chairs. Switch off the lights. Hold the puppet close to the cloth and shine a torch from behind it. Look from the front.
flow.kid: Hang the cloth. Hold the puppet close behind it. Shine a torch from behind. Look from the front.
flow.parent: The puppet must be close to the screen to make a sharp shadow. Hold the torch about a metre behind the puppet. Make the room dim, and shine the torch so that it lights the screen from behind. If the coloured windows look dim, make the room darker and move the torch closer to the puppet.
flow.wait: Leave the glue to dry until tomorrow, then continue.
flow.context: In this step, you hang the screen and make a first test.

flow.do: Perform a short show with a white torch behind the screen. Make each puppet walk, fly or dance. Look at the screen from the front and see the dark body and the coloured windows.
flow.say: Perform a small show with the white torch. What do you see on the screen? What colour is each window? What colour is the body?
flow.kid: Put on a show with the white torch. What colours do the windows show?
flow.parent: With a white torch, the dark body of the puppet blocks the light, and each cellophane window lets through its own colour. This is the same as red cellophane on a torch, but smaller. One child: the child works the puppet and the parent holds the torch. With 2 to 4 children: one holds the torch, one or two work puppets, and one watches from the front and writes what each window looks like. Swap jobs for each show.
flow.context: In this step, you perform a short show with a white torch and look at the colours.

flow.do: Now cover the torch with green cellophane and perform again. Look at the red window. Then cover the torch with red cellophane and look at the green window. Write down what each window looks like.
flow.say: Now a green torch behind the screen. What does the red window look like now? Then try a red torch. What does the green window look like?
flow.kid: Use a green torch. What does the red window look like? Then use a red torch and look at the green window.

check.q: Through a green torch, the red window looked almost black. Why?
options: The red cellophane lets red light through, and the green torch has almost no red to give it
The green torch is too weak
Red cellophane turns green light black
check.why: A red filter only lets red light through. A green torch gives almost no red, so almost no light gets past the red window. Picking 'too weak' might feel right, but the green window glows brightly in the same light. Picking 'turns light black' sounds like a trick, but the cellophane only holds back light.

flow.context: In this step, you shine coloured light through windows of another colour.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they found out, using the puppets as evidence. Ask what they would change if they did it again.
flow.say: Tell me what you found. Which window was brightest in white light? Which one went dark in coloured light? Why?
flow.kid: Tell me what you found out. Which window went dark? Why?
flow.think: A shadow puppet show is just a way of putting a filter in a beam of light. What other things around us are filters?
flow.context: In this step, you finish like a scientist, by telling what you found.

challenges.title: Eight Looks From Three Torches
challenges.problem: You have a red torch, a green torch and a blue torch, and a white wall. Make as many different colours on the wall as you can, using only these three. Find out how many different looks the wall can have, and write down the recipe for each.
constraints: Use only red, green and blue cellophane. No other colours of paper, paint or pens.
Each torch is either on or off, with nothing in between, for the main count.
Write the recipe each time, for example red and green.
Keep the torches the same distance from the wall for the main count, and keep the room dim.
materials: three torches, or three phone torches (borrow from the family if you need to)
red, green and blue cellophane, held over each torch with rubber bands (two layers for red and green, one layer for blue, which is dim)
a plain white wall, or a big sheet of white card
a dim room, such as a room with the curtains closed in the evening
paper and a pencil for the recipes
general: Switch on one torch at a time: red, then green, then blue.
Switch on two torches at a time: red and green, green and blue, red and blue.
Switch on all three torches, and switch off all three.
creative: Move one torch further away so that it is fainter, and see how the colour changes. Orange is a red torch strong and a green torch weak.
Fold the cellophane into three layers on one torch to dim it, and mix again.
Set up a little light show with a sequence of looks, and give each look a name, like sunrise, sea and sunset.
challenges.your_turn: Make your own list of looks. Draw a picture of each and write the recipe. How many different looks did you make? Can you make a colour that is not on anyone else's list?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about mixing coloured light. You find out how many different colours three torches can make on a wall.

setup.art: Three torches with red, green and blue cellophane, pointing at a white wall, with a table to write the recipes on.
setup.caption: 1. Set up three coloured torches facing a white wall.

setup.art: A white wall with eight small drawings of its looks: dark, red, green, blue, yellow, cyan, magenta and white.
setup.caption: 2. Try every on and off setting. Write down each look.

setup.art: A child moving one torch further from the wall and a pale orange patch on the wall.
setup.caption: 3. Change one thing. What new colour do you get?

flow.do: Read the challenge together. Ask your child how many different looks there will be. Ask how they can be sure they found them all.
flow.say: Here is your job. Three torches. Red, green and blue. Each one on or off. How many different looks can you make on the wall? How can you be sure you found them all?
flow.kid: Three torches. Each one on or off. How many looks can you make?

ask.q: How can you be sure you found every look?
good: Try each torch on its own, then pairs, then all three.
Write a list and tick them off.
Check each torch is on or off in every try.

flow.parent: Let your child make a plan. A good plan is a list, so no setting is missed. Do not give the answer.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Eight Looks challenge. You read the problem and make a plan.

flow.do: Try every setting of the three torches and write the recipe and the colour for each. Include the setting with all three torches off. Check whether any recipes give the same look.
flow.say: Try every setting. Write the recipe and the colour. Do not forget the setting with all three off. Tick each one off your list.
flow.kid: Try every setting. Write the recipe and the colour. Tick each one off.
flow.parent: Expect eight looks: dark, red, green, blue, yellow (red and green), cyan (green and blue), magenta (red and blue) and white. Some may look slightly different from these because cheap cellophane is not pure. Write what you really see. Prop phones on a pile of books so your hands are free. With only two torches, swap the cellophane between them to try the pairs: red and green, green and blue, red and blue. You will miss white until you borrow a third light. One child: the parent holds one torch. 2 to 4 children: give each child a torch and one child writes the recipes, then swap.

check.q: Three torches are each on or off. How many different settings are there, counting all off?
check.why: Each torch has 2 choices, on or off. For three torches, that is 2 times 2 times 2, which is 8. The settings are: all off, three with one torch, three with two torches, and one with all three. Picking 6 forgets all off and all on. Picking 9 is a guess.

flow.context: In this step, you try each on and off setting and write down the colours.

flow.do: Now change one thing at a time. Move a torch further away, or add another layer of cellophane to it. Look at the new colours. Try to make orange and pink. Write down what you did each time.
flow.say: Now invent. Move a torch back, or add another layer. Can you make orange? Can you make pink? Write what you did.
flow.kid: Move a torch back or add a layer. Can you make orange? Pink?
flow.parent: Orange comes from a strong red and a weak green. Pink comes from a strong red with weaker green and blue. Changing the distance of a torch changes how much light it adds. Change only one thing at a time, so you know what made the difference.
flow.context: In this step, you invent new colours by changing how strong each torch is.

flow.do: Show your family a short light show of your best looks. Name each look and say its recipe. Ask them to guess the recipe before you tell them.
flow.say: Put on a light show. Name each look. Can your family guess the recipe before you tell them?
flow.kid: Show your family a light show. Say each recipe.
flow.think: Three torches made eight looks. How many looks would four torches make, with each one on or off?
flow.context: In this step, you show your family your looks and explain the recipes.

quiz.p: Which three colours of light make white when they are shone together on one spot of a white wall?
quiz.why: Red, green and blue lights add up to white. Red, yellow and blue are the old painters' set. Cyan, magenta and yellow are the three inks of a printer.

quiz.p: A pencil stands in front of a wall lit by a red torch and a green torch. What colour is the shadow where the red light is blocked?
quiz.why: Where the red light is blocked, only the green light still reaches the wall, so the shadow looks green.

quiz.p: A yellow sheet and a cyan sheet are held together in front of a white torch. What colour comes out?
quiz.why: Yellow lets red and green through. Cyan lets green and blue through. Only green gets past both. Each sheet takes colours away.

quiz.p: A blue shirt is lit by a pure red light. What does it look like?
quiz.why: The shirt sends back blue light. A pure red light has almost no blue, so the shirt has little to send back.

quiz.p: Why can just three lights make so many colours?
opts: Most eyes have three kinds of cone cell, and colour is built from their three signals
Three is a magic number in nature
The lights hide the other colours inside them
quiz.why: The eye turns all light into three signals. Lights that give the right three signals can look like any colour.

quiz.p: A newspaper photo is made of tiny dots of four inks. Why does it look like a smooth picture from a metre away?
opts: The dots are too small and close to tell apart, so their light blends in the eye
quiz.why: Your eye cannot tell tiny dots apart from far away. Their light lands on the same cone cells and adds up.

quiz.p: Which sentence is the best reasoning for 'red and green torches make a yellow wall'?
opts: Each torch adds light to the wall, and the eye gives the same answer to red plus green as to yellow
Red and green paint make yellow
There was yellow hiding in the torches
quiz.why: Reasoning says why. It uses what lights do and what the eye does. It does not use paint, because paint takes colours away.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists not know yet?
opts: How three signals in the brain become the feeling of a colour
That red and green light look yellow together
quiz.why: The first two were tested many times. How signals become a feeling is still an open question.

quiz.p: Which two lights shining together make magenta?
quiz.why: Red plus blue light makes magenta. Red plus green makes yellow. Green plus blue makes cyan.

quiz.p: You stare at a bright green shape and then see a pink ghost on a white wall. What made the pink?
opts: Tired cone cells in your eye
A pink spot on the wall
quiz.why: The cone cells that sense green tired while you stared. On white they answered less than usual, so the white looked a little pink.

quiz.p: A yellow cloth is held in blue light. What does it look like?
quiz.why: Yellow cloth sends back red and green, and a blue light has almost none of either.

quiz.p: Cyan ink and yellow ink are printed on the same spot of a page. What colour does the spot look?
quiz.why: Cyan ink takes away red and yellow ink takes away blue. Only green is left.

applications: Phones, TVs and computer screens make every colour, and white, from tiny red, green and blue dots.
Stage and film lighting designers use red, green and blue lamps and colour filters to set the mood of a scene.
Colour printers make full-colour pictures from cyan, magenta, yellow and black ink.
Boats show a red light on the left and a green light on the right at night, so that other boats can tell which way they are heading.
Traffic signals use red, amber and green lights, so the colours are easy to tell apart from far away.
Wedding and festival LED strip lights change colour by changing how bright their red, green and blue lamps are.
Photographers and phone cameras use a setting called white balance, so that a white thing looks white under any lamp.
Dyers and weavers in India check cloth colours in daylight, because lamps change how colours look.
Colour vision tests help find people who need help with colour-coded jobs, such as wiring or reading maps.
Painters such as Georges Seurat built whole pictures from small dots of colour that blend in the eye.
Sunglasses and camera filters take away some light or some colours before the light reaches the eye or the sensor.
Cross-stitch and weaving patterns put threads of different colours side by side, so that the colours mix in the eye from a distance.

open_questions.q: How do three signals from cone cells turn into the feeling of yellow?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can follow the signals from the eye into the brain. But nobody knows how those signals become the feeling of a colour. Some call this the hard problem.

open_questions.q: Does your yellow feel the same as my yellow?
open_questions.why_open: We can test whether two people sort colours the same way. We cannot yet find a way to compare what a colour feels like from the inside.

open_questions.q: Could a person ever see a colour that nobody has seen before?
open_questions.why_open: In the 1980s a few experiments reported that people saw colours such as reddish green when the eyes were tricked in a special way. Other scientists want these results repeated.

open_questions.q: What do birds with four kinds of cone cell see that we cannot?
open_questions.why_open: We can measure what their eyes respond to and test what they can tell apart. We cannot imagine the experience, and we cannot ask them.

open_questions.q: How exactly does the brain take away the colour of the light, so that a white sheet looks white under a yellow lamp?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know the brain compares different parts of a scene. They are still working out how, and why some people guess differently, as with the famous photo of a dress.

open_questions.q: Why do most people have three kinds of cone cell, and not two or four?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists think three helped our early ancestors tell ripe fruit from leaves. But the full story of why we ended up with three is still being pieced together.

open_questions.q: Do colours feel calm or excited in the same way for everyone?
open_questions.why_open: Some studies find that people in many places link red with warmth and blue with calm. Others find that it changes from place to place and from culture to culture.

ask_kids: If a red lamp and a green lamp shine on the same wall, what colour do you think the wall will be?
Which of your clothes would look different under a street lamp at night?
Why do you think a shopkeeper takes a sari to the door?
Can you find something in the kitchen that looks different in sunlight and under a bulb?
What colour do you think a green mango looks under a red bulb?
If a dog sees fewer colours than you, what do you think is easier for a dog to see?
Look at a phone screen from close up and from far away. What changes?
What colours do you think your shadow could be, if two lamps of different colours were on?
If you could add a fourth kind of colour cell to your eyes, what do you think would change?
Why do you think printers use black ink as well as cyan, magenta and yellow?
Is white a colour, or is it all the colours together? What do you think?

jokes.j: What did the cyan say to the yellow?
Why was the pencil's shadow green?
jokes.a: It was green with envy of the red one.

jokes.j: What happens when a red torch tells a joke to a green torch?

maths.problem: In the Eight Looks challenge, three torches are each on or off, which gives 8 settings. A school stage has four lamps instead of three, each on or off. How many settings does it have, counting all off? Explain how you worked it out.
maths.explain: Three lamps give 8 settings. A fourth lamp can be on or off with each of those 8 settings. So there are 8 settings with it off and 8 with it on. 8 plus 8 is 16. Each new lamp doubles the settings.
maths.context: In this challenge, you try every on and off setting of three torches and count the different looks.
maths.why_maths: Counting all the settings in an organised way shows that you have found them all, and lets you predict how many a bigger set of lamps would give.

maths.problem: In the Highlighter Layers grid there are 9 crossing squares. 3 of them are crossings of the same colour with itself. What fraction of the crossing squares are crossings of two different colours?
maths.answer: 6 out of 9, which is the same as two thirds.
maths.explain: There are 9 squares in all. 3 of them are the same colour twice. So 9 take away 3 is 6 squares with two different colours. 6 out of 9 can be shared by 3, which gives 2 out of 3.
maths.context: In this experiment, you draw three stripes across three other stripes and look at the nine crossing squares.
maths.why_maths: A fraction tells you how much of the grid shows new colours, so you can say that most of your results are new mixes.

maths.problem: A phone screen row is 1,000 pixels wide. Each pixel has one red, one green and one blue dot across. How many coloured dots are there along one row?
maths.explain: Each pixel has 3 dots. There are 1,000 pixels. 1,000 times 3 is 3,000. So there are 3,000 coloured dots along one row.
maths.context: In this activity, you find that a printed picture is made of tiny dots, and that a screen is too.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying shows how tiny each dot must be, which is why your eye cannot tell them apart and their light blends.

maths.problem: In the Wrong-Colour Flag test, Meera stared at 3 pictures for 30 seconds each, and rested her eyes for 20 seconds between them. How long did the whole test take?
maths.answer: 130 seconds, which is 2 minutes and 10 seconds.
maths.explain: Three stares of 30 seconds make 90 seconds. There are 2 rests between 3 pictures, and 2 times 20 is 40 seconds. 90 plus 40 is 130 seconds. 130 seconds is 2 minutes and 10 seconds.
maths.context: In this activity, you stare at a picture for 30 seconds and then look at a white wall.
maths.why_maths: Adding the stares and the rests tells you how long to plan for, and shows that the eye needs rests.

maths.problem: In one test, thin stripes blended into one colour when you stood 3 metres away. Stripes that were twice as wide blended at 6 metres. At what distance would stripes three times as wide blend?
maths.explain: Twice as wide gave twice the distance, 6 metres. So the distance goes up in step with the width. Three times as wide means three times the distance. 3 times 3 is 9 metres.
maths.context: In this activity, you draw thin stripes and walk away until they blend into one colour.
maths.why_maths: Seeing that the distance grows with the width lets you predict a result you have not measured, and then test whether you were right.

maths.problem: Eight people did the Wrong-Colour Flag test. The chart shows how many saw the ghost flag clearly, faintly or not at all. How many people saw it at all? What fraction saw it clearly?
maths.answer: 7 people saw it at all. 5 out of 8 saw it clearly.
maths.explain: 5 saw it clearly and 2 saw it faintly. 5 plus 2 is 7. The 1 person who saw nothing is not counted. 5 of the 8 people saw it clearly, so the fraction is 5 out of 8.
maths.context: In this activity, family members stare at a flag drawn in the wrong colours and then look at a white wall.

chart.title: Made-up example: how many people saw the ghost flag

maths.why_maths: A chart shows at a glance that most people saw it, but not everyone, which tells you afterimages vary from eye to eye.

maths.problem: A designer says orange needs 3 units of red light for every 1 unit of green light. A big curtain gets 12 units of red light. How many units of green light does it need for the same orange?
maths.explain: For every 3 units of red there is 1 unit of green. 12 units of red is 4 groups of 3. So there are 4 groups of 1 unit of green, which is 4 units.
maths.context: In this challenge, you make orange by using a strong red torch and a weak green torch.
maths.why_maths: A ratio lets a designer keep the same colour when the light gets stronger, by keeping the same shares.

maths.problem: A torch gives 100 units of light. A yellow sheet lets half of the light through. A second yellow sheet lets half of what is left through. How many units reach the wall with one sheet, with two sheets and with three sheets?
maths.answer: 50 units with one sheet, 25 units with two sheets and 12 and a half units with three sheets.
maths.explain: Half of 100 is 50. Half of 50 is 25. Half of 25 is 12 and a half. Each sheet halves what is left, so the light gets weaker with every sheet.
maths.context: In this experiment, you layer highlighter inks and see that each layer takes some light away.
maths.why_maths: Halving again and again shows why a stack of filters or inks gets darker quickly, and why many paints mixed together look nearly black.

roots.context: We have mixed coloured lights, stacked coloured inks and watched colours vanish and appear. Now we ask what these tests tell us about colour itself, and about the eye that sees it.

deep_truth.truth: The wall lit by a red torch and a green torch looked yellow, yet no yellow light reached it. Your eye has only three kinds of colour sensor, so it reports red plus green as yellow. Very different mixes of light can feel exactly the same to us. So a colour is what your eye reports, not something the light has.
deep_truth.habit: We say a lemon sends yellow light, as if each colour name were one fixed kind of light. But red plus green and real yellow are different light that look the same. A colour name tells us about the eye as much as about the light.
deep_truth.evidence: In the two torch test, the wall looked yellow where the red and green lights overlapped, though only a red torch and a green torch were on. If your wall looked orange or greenish, write that down honestly. Cheap cellophane is never perfect, and your result is still real evidence.

three.who_am_i: Every colour you have ever seen came from just three signals in your eyes. You are partly made of how your own eyes answer the light.
three.what_is_life: Different kinds of animals have different numbers of colour cells. A dog has two kinds, most people have three and many birds have four. Each kind of animal lives in a set of colours of their own.
three.what_is_this_world: The world sends out light of every wavelength. Each eye picks just a few signals from it. So the colours we know are a meeting between the world and an eye.

roots.thread: Light comes in a whole range of wavelengths. An eye sorts that range into only three signals, and everything we call colour is built from those three. That is why three lights can stand in for almost any mix. The red and green torches did not turn into yellow. Your eyes gave the same answer to them as to real yellow. So colour lives in the meeting of light and a living eye, and neither makes it alone.

teachings.teaching: Plotinus, a Greek thinker who lived about 1,800 years ago, wrote that no eye could ever see the Sun unless it had first become something like the Sun.
teachings.link: Our eyes are built to catch sunlight, which holds all the colours. Each kind of cone cell is tuned to a different part of it.

teachings.teaching: The Katha Upanishad says that there the Sun does not shine, nor the Moon or the stars, nor this lightning. All things shine after that light, and by its light all this is lit.
teachings.link: Every colour in a room is lit by a light that comes first. Without light, a rose, a leaf and a wall have no colour to show.

teachings.teaching: Laozi wrote that the five colours make the eyes blind. He meant that a mind dazzled by bright things stops seeing what is quiet underneath.
teachings.link: A brightly coloured stage can fool the eye. A red and a green lamp made a yellow that was not there.

science.text: Most people have three kinds of cone cell, and lights that excite the three kinds in the same way look the same. Thomas Young proposed this in 1802, and later experiments confirmed it.
How three signals in the brain become the feeling of a colour, such as yellow, is not known.

other_view.view: Real yellow light and red-plus-green light are different things. One has a single wavelength and the other has two. A spectrometer tells them apart at once. So the colour is in the light, and the eye is just a poor instrument that can be fooled.

practice.title: Is white always white?
practice.say: Sit near a window in the daytime with a plain sheet of white paper. Hold the paper up, and look at it for three slow breaths. Notice its colour. Now carry the paper under a yellowish lamp, and look for three more breaths. Notice its colour again. Last, ask yourself which colour the paper really is. Let that question sit in your mind while you breathe out slowly.
practice.kid: Look at a white page by the window. Breathe in and out three times. Now look at it under a lamp. Breathe three times. Is it the same white? Which one is real?

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet done at home. Two Torches, Two Shadows: this is the core test. It needs a dim room, two torches or phone torches, and red and green cellophane or sweet wrappers. Cheap cellophane lets some white light through, so the colours are a little pale. The overlap often looks orange or yellow-green, not pure yellow, and the step tells you how to balance it by moving a torch back. The shadows are faint in a bright room, so do it in the evening with the curtains closed. Highlighter Layers: the crossings of yellow and blue, pink and yellow, and pink and blue give green, orange-red and purple with most highlighters. A three-layer patch is dark. Brands differ, so the table asks for what you really see. The Wrong-Colour Flag works for most people, but the ghost is faint and short. The step says to stare for 30 seconds and to try 45 seconds if nothing appears. Stripes That Blend: the distance at which fine pen stripes blend depends on the pen and on your eyes. A corridor or a terrace helps. Navy or Black needs daylight and one warm light (a warm bulb, or a phone torch with yellow cellophane). Many homes have LED bulbs of different warmth, so any two will do. Games and projects: Add or Take Away has 24 cards and 8 tokens and works with 2 to 4 players. The puppet show needs a grown-up to cut windows. Never look at the Sun through cellophane. Numbers to check before sharing: about 1 boy or man in 12 and about 1 girl or woman in 200 have a colour vision difference. Dogs have two kinds of cone cell and many birds have four. These are widely reported figures and are worth checking against a recent source.
